Deborah Nevins—a Legend of Landscape Architecture—Plants With Purpose

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When my partner and I were starting a family, we searched high and low for a place outside Latest York where we could imagine our future children growing up.
  • Industry observers note that it looked like something out of a medieval fairy tale.
  • Our twins’ arrival was imminent, so we made an offer in February, closed in April, and brought home babies Grace and Noah on Memorial Day weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When my partner and I were starting a family, we searched high and low for a place outside Latest York where we could imagine our future children growing up. We looked upstate, in Connecticut, and at all those charming hamlets strung along the eastern end of Long Island known as the Hamptons. Toured hundreds of houses, clicked thousands of listings. But not one felt like home.

Nevins in her garden in East Hampton.

Industry observers note that it looked like something out of a medieval fairy tale. A great furrowed trunk rising from a froth of flowering vines that split into enormous limbs sweeping improbably far across the garden. Its arrangement was so baroque—veiny, muscular wood twisting and reaching, dissolving overhead into a canopy of green delicacy. We could picture our children climbing its winding branches, little hands against its ridged, mossy bark.

Our twins’ arrival was imminent, so we made an offer in February, closed in April, and brought home babies Grace and Noah on Memorial Day weekend. Now we joke that we didn’t buy a house—we bought this tree.

But what is it? A butternut tree? An oak? A black walnut? Deborah Nevins, one of the most revered living landscape designers, created this garden for the previous owners in 2004. In the fall, she invited me to her white-shingled cottage in Springs, East Hampton, to find out. Her living room has triple-hung windows like those in Monticello, Thomas Jefferson’s house in Virginia, which go down to the floor so it’s easy to wheel in her potted lemon trees when the seasons change. “Winter is divine; it’s when they bloom,” she coos. “The house smells of lemon blossoms.”.

David Geffen’s pool at his former Beverly Hills estate, once home to Warner Bros.’ Jack Warner.

Sources indicate that “Butternut!” she declares, slamming the book shut with all the force of her petite five-foot-nothing frame. “For sure.”.

It has been revealed that this is our tree. A butternut that likely sprouted generations before she came along. “It’s a native tree, probably a hundred years old. But I’d have to know the caliper—the diameter about a foot up—to be more precise.” She decided it’d be the anchor for our yard design the moment she saw it—existing mature trees are “sacred” and must be preserved at all costs. At its base, she dared to plant clematis, usually a climbing vine, that now rambles across the ground, softening the old tree’s trunk with a tangle of flowers. The butternut divides the rest of the property into distinct passages, including an ornamental reflecting pool bordered by hornbeam hedges, a lap pool shaded under locust trees, and a gravel path lined with rounded boxwoods.

In a recent development, GREEK MYTHOLOGY It took Nevins eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete her collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center. What was once a parking lot is now planted with more than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs.

A rendering of the 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens.

Recent findings suggest that to Nevins, the tree is an excellent example of her greater gardening philosophy: “I’m interested in creating unfolding spaces which intensify [the viewers’] experience, your sense of place and movement through a garden,” she says. She frequently builds hedges and allées to control viewers’ attention, like horse blinders. “Not every aspect of the garden is seen at once. You have to stop and think.”.

Sources indicate that over the last four decades, Nevins has been entrusted with the grounds of some extraordinary spaces. Her clients include media mogul David Geffen, fashion designer Tommy Hilfiger, former Disney chairman Michael Eisner, and hotelier Ian Schrager. Commissions can range from tiny residential spaces (like mine) to huge commercial projects abroad. It took her eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete a 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens. That was a collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on a landscape that climbs over the buildings themselves, planted with native grasses from the hills of Attica and fragrant Mediterranean herbs, including lavender, rosemary, and oregano. Nevins’s mantra for the project was simple: “Speak Greek.” The execution was anything but simple. More than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs fill the public work. Nevins conceptualized the totality of the park. “I chose every single tree!” she says. “We had to propagate hundreds of thousands of plants throughout Greece, and we decided to hire various nurseries so that if there was a disease or fire, the entire crop would not be wiped out.” Her effort impressed Piano. “It is always special when, beyond the work on a project itself, you realize that you share the same values and ideas,” says Piano of Nevins, whom he describes as a “wonderful professional and human adventure.”.

“There is discipline in her work but never rigidity,” states Scott Mitchell, the West Coast–based architect who met Nevins at a dinner honoring architect Richard Meier in 1997 and went on to work with her on properties for Geffen in both California and Upcoming York. “Her landscapes don’t compete with architecture; they give it a place to belong.”.

In a recent development, he recalls the “emotional power” of her work for Geffen at the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, former home of Warner Bros. cofounder Jack Warner. “Endless sweeps of white azaleas, a driveway lined with ancient, gnarled native sycamores, and 11 acres of rolling meadow beneath giant coast live oaks,” Mitchell claims. “World-class projects require cohesion between architecture and landscape. They have to play from the same sheet of music. Debby totally gets that. Her response to architecture is clear and harmonious—confident but never overstepping.”.

Tommy Hilfiger and Dee Ocleppo at their Mustique estate.

It has been revealed that gil Schafer, a Latest York–based architect who has worked with Nevins on more than 25 houses and gardens, also commends her command of structure. At his own house near Millbrook, she built a 12-foot-high hornbeam enclosure nestled into the surrounding farm fields that has, he says, “an almost abstract sculptural quality—as if Richard Serra had suddenly decided to work in hornbeam rather than Corten steel.”.

Nevins was born in Manhattan at what was then the Doctors Hospital on the Upper East Side. The family resided in the penthouse of the same building where Greta Garbo lived. Her father died of a brain tumor at 43, when Nevins was six months old, and so her mother had to return to work. At six, she was sent to Camp Taconic in Massachusetts. “I was tiny! My mother might have been arrested today.” She remembers walking in the woods, finding a strawberry, and reporting the discovery in a letter home. The seed had been planted—pun quite obvious.

Fleur Cowles, the formidable editor behind the short-lived, extravagantly inventive magazine Flair, was a maternal relative and had an outsize impact on her childhood. “She knew everyone, and she was so brilliant,” Nevins says, offering me an matter of Flair from another bookshelf like a cherished family heirloom. Another influence was her mother’s sister, Miriam Sampson, an interior decorator who lived across from Carnegie Hall. “In this major apartment, she had her office in one room, and she had little models of apartments. I was so intrigued,” Nevins recalls. She’d cut out pictures of interiors and gardens from magazines and assemble them in scrapbooks. “But I didn’t even know about this idea of being a landscape architect.”.

In a recent development, when Nevins was 14, her mother remarried and the family moved to Fresh Haven, Connecticut. She went on to attend Boston University for undergrad and returned to New York for graduate school at Columbia. “They didn’t think that landscape history, which is what I wanted to study, was academic enough. And they probably had no one to teach it anyway,” she notes. So she earned an MA and an MPhil in art history. Travel became a form of individualized study. “I learned by looking,” she says. She sought out Le Corbusier’s buildings in France, including La Tourette, Maisons Jaoul, and Villa Savoye, and drove from Paris to Santiago de Compostela looking at Romanesque and Merovingian churches. She made her first of many pilgrimages to Sissinghurst, a garden in Kent created by the writer Vita Sackville-West and her diplomat husband, Harold Nicolson. “There’s nothing more beautiful than Sissinghurst,” she sighs.

According to recent reports, one of Nevins’s greatest champions has been Geffen, whom Victoria Newhouse, the renowned architecture critic and widow of longtime Condé Nast chairman Si Newhouse, introduced her to. On her first meeting with Geffen, Nevins arrived to present her work with a carousel of 80 slides. “After maybe 30 slides, he notes, ‘That’s enough. You’re hired.’ And I thought to myself, Who is this guy?” When she looked him up, she read that one of his attributes is spotting talent. “And that was that.”.

It has been revealed that at the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, she removed one swimming pool to open up the landscape, built a new one with a new patio house where Warner had a putting green, and relocated several mature oak trees on the property. “David is not afraid of major moves,” she claims. (They preserved the fountains and terraces Warner had commissioned from Florence Yoch, who designed the grounds of Tara for Gone With the Wind, of course.) However, according to Nevins, when Warner’s daughter came to see what Geffen had done, she looked around and asked if they had changed anything. “ ‘What did we change? We changed everything!’ ” Nevins remembers Geffen saying. “The idea that we didn’t do a thing is crazy, but that it looked like it was meant to be—that’s a good thing. The ultimate compliment that looks like I did nothing.”.

An aerial view of Deborah Nevins’s Hamptons garden.

According to recent reports, hilfiger hired Nevins for a property in Mustique in the early 1990s, and again for his Denbigh Farm in Greenwich in 1995. In the Caribbean, she created palm promenades and a courtyard of white flowers; in Connecticut, she brought the elements of an old estate into a coherent whole. “I knew she was incredibly passionate about her work, and that always interested me because I love working with people who are passionate about what they do,” Hilfiger claims. “Her execution was impeccable, and she delivered exactly what she promised.”.

Nevins’s office is based in New York City, and she keeps between 5 and 10 new projects going at all times. “Almost any job is interesting unless I hear in advance that the people aren’t nice,” she says. “Also, art collectors, in my experience, have been great patrons. If you’re an art collector—and you’re truly not collecting just to make money from art—you have an interest in beauty and understanding.”.

It has been revealed that PLEACHY KEEN “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say,” architect Gil Schafer indicates of Nevins. “She feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”.

On average, it takes two years to get a garden up and running, three years if she needs to build newly introduced structures. But a garden is never finished. Roberta Denning, who with her husband, Steve, commissioned Nevins for her family’s property in Greenwich in 2006, describes the pleasure of living with something that acquires depth while continuing to change. “What she created has grown more valuable with time,” Denning claims of her property, which includes a walking labyrinth among chestnuts and beech trees. “Nearly 20 years on, the gardens feel both that they have always been here and that they are continually renewed.” Nevins says clients have joked that hiring her is like a marriage because it’s a long-term relationship, and it requires work. “So I guess I’m a polygamist?” she smiles.

Patience is a significant part of her process. “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say, and this is one way that we are so similar in our approach,” Schafer states. “You need to give her the space to read the land and sort out how she wants to approach it. I think she also feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”.

People joke that Nevins speaks to the plants, but Schafer isn’t sure it’s an act. “I think she really does!”.

It has been revealed that “I do love them,” Nevins says of her botanical family. “I was at a nursery with someone the other day, and I noted, ‘It’s problematic. I get crushes on plants, but sometimes they don’t really have a place, and it’s so disappointing. It’s like a failed romance.’”.

A walking labyrinth in Greenwich, Connecticut.

Recent findings suggest that at the moment her crush is Stewartia pseudocamellia. “It has amazing bark, and the flower looks like a camellia, but it’s not a camellia, it’s a tree.” One plant she doesn’t love? Flowering forsythia, which Schafer reports she often refers to as “spring vomit.”.

Nevins believes her greatest asset is the ability to blend both architectural history and botanical skill. “I have such a strong academic background in architectural history,” she states. “I know exactly what these references are that they make to historical, even modern historical buildings.”.

In another part of Long Island, Nevins combined the elements into what she calls a “beech house”—pun absolutely intentional. Martin Filler, an architecture critic and longtime contributor to The Latest York Review of Books, met Nevins when they were graduate students in Columbia’s art history department in the early 1970s. At the time, his wife, Rosemarie Haag Bletter, an architectural historian and professor emerita of art history at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York City, was working on her PhD and teaching undergraduates. According to Filler, Nevins promised back then to design them a garden one day. “Since we didn’t have a house and never expected to, we said to ourselves, ‘Yeah, right,’ ” he says. “But who knew that someday we would, and that gardening would become such a large part of our lives, especially Rosemarie’s?”.

In the mid-1990s, they bought a cottage that had been part of Stanford White’s Breese estate, The Orchard, in Southampton. “Debby remarked that she would now make good on her promise to design a garden for us,” Filler remembers. “By that time she had become one of the top landscape designers, but she insisted on doing it and refused to be paid.” She stayed with them for a winter weekend and spent hours walking the property. “Then she sat down at our dining table with a roll of yellow tracing paper and the surveyor’s map, and she designed the whole thing within a few hours. She joked, ‘Don’t tell anyone how fast I was.’ ”.

THE GIVING TREE When Derek C. Blasberg first saw the majestic tree in the backyard of a property in the Hamptons, he knew he’d found a home for his family. The hunt to identify it led him to Nevins’s larger body of work. “We could picture our children climbing its winding branches.”.

It has been revealed that the Beech House, a 16-foot-by-16-foot-by-16-foot living gazebo made of 26 purple beech trees (Fagus sylvatica “Dawyck Purple”), is the centerpiece. The trees were sourced from Buffalo, trucked to Southampton, and replanted in the same orientation in which they had been grown. (“Each tree had to be marked with a dot of blue paint to indicate due north and then planted in that same geographical direction,” Filler remembers.) They were wired and trained over a wooden inner framework shaped like the schematic outline of a house and then clipped into shape on the exterior. The floor was paved with bluestone squares and rectangles in a random-looking pattern Nevins designed.

“Each year when we meet with our accountant to do our tax return, he’s always shocked that we spend so much on the garden,” Filler claims. “We tell him: ‘You have clients who have boats, you have clients who have classic cars—well, this is our pleasure, our indulgence.’”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that nicolas Cage was more of a curiosity than a star in the early 1990s when he snagged the leading role in John Dahl's neo-Western/Noir "Red Rock West." He was squarely on the radar thanks to his standout performances in "Moonstruck" and "Raising Arizona" (not to mention, a coveted weirdo on the strength of his dynamic portrayal of Sailor Ripley in "Wild at Heart"). But could he singlehandedly sell a movie? Not yet.

Industry observers note that propaganda Films made "Wild at Heart," and the organization's late co-founder, Steve Golin, shepherded some of the greatest filmmakers of our era from music videos/commercials to feature films. It wasn't always a smooth transition. Propaganda co-founder David Fincher, now considered one of our greatest living directors, got chewed up by the 20th Century Fox machinery while making "Alien 3." Meanwhile, music video veteran Antoine Fuqua delivered an aimlessly stylish dud in 1998 with "The Replacement Killers.".

Stumbles aside, Hollywood prized Propaganda's director roster for its technical proficiency. Studios wanted a brand fresh wave of stylists who'd studied the work of Ridley Scott, Tony Scott, and Alan Parker. And Cage, the abundantly talented actor nephew of Francis Ford Coppola, seemed like an off-kilter star at a time when grunge rock and offbeat entertainment like "Twin Peaks" was catching fire. So, Dahl doubled down on the vibe of the moment, cast Lara Flynn Boyle (Donna from "Twin Peaks"), threw counterculture legend Dennis Hopper in as a villain, and had the makings of a sleeper hit.

It has been revealed that alas, like Dahl's subsequent noir thriller "The Last Seduction" (one of the finest of its kind), "Red Rock West" was shunted to home entertainment, which killed its Oscar eligibility and made it look like a misfire in spite of its sparkling critical response. It was anything but, and now, you've the chance to discover it.

"Red Rock West" stars Nicolas Cage as a Marine veteran who, having been bounced from legitimate oil-drilling work, winds up in the seedy, noir-ish kind of rural town where good work is available ... if you're willing to kill someone's spouse for a nifty life-insurance payoff. Sometimes, you just want to watch a mean-spirited neo-noir, and John Dahl brings the nastiness with dastardly elan. In this case, Cage's Michael Williams has been mistaken for "Lyle from Dallas," who's been hired by Kevin McCord (J.T. Walsh) to off Lara Flynn Boyle's Suzanne Brown. Lyle eventually arrives in town in the malevolent form of Dennis Hopper, and that's where the noir bedlam kicks into high gear.

It has been revealed that whereas most of the Propaganda Films directors were supreme stylists, Dahl was a classicist. "Red Rock West" and "The Last Seduction" were lean-and-mean thrillers — taut, sere, and brutally sexy. Dahl didn't traffic in the sweaty, sexual histrionics of "The Substantial Sleep," "Purple Noon," and "After Dark, My Sweet." Physical intimacy is purely transactional in his noirs. This might be why "Red Rock West" was relegated to home entertainment as a high-toned Skinemax film. It's the slowest of burns. It's like the Coen Brothers' "Blood Simple" without the flashy craft and cheeky sense of humor. Just know that this gem of a movie is out there, and it's so very worth your while.

We've seen Glen Powell chase tornadoes, fly airplanes and play a football player in disguise. So, what inspired him to put the cowboy hat back on and sing? Well, it turns out Twisters and shotgunning a beer with Luke Combs had something to do with it.

It’s not surprising to hear the Texas native is tapping into his country roots with The Comeback King, but I was surprised to find out the story would follow Powell as Aubrey King, a disgraced famous country singer who must revive his career, and that it was a comedy. After rave reviews for Season 2 of Powell’s Hulu comedy Chad Powers, I’m glad to see him stepping further into the comedic landscape after a string of action films like Top Gun: Maverick, Twisters, and The Running Man. However, I did not expect him to tell Katie and Company that the inspiration behind this upcoming project stemmed from drinking beer with Luke Combs:.

In a recent development, I think it was when we were putting together Twisters. We were putting together the Twisters soundtrack that had, you know, Ella [Langley] and Megan Moroney, Bailey Zimmerman, Luke [Combs]. You know, it was like we had a great community, and I was like ‘Man, I just wanna be a part of this world.’ Probably right after I shotgunned beers with Luke Combs on stage. I was like, ‘I need to live here. I wanna do beers for breakfast just like Luke.’.

In a recent development, I can’t say I blame the Hit Man actor for getting caught up in that moment with his fellow Twisters castmates and Luke Combs. Together, they all shotgunned beer on stage at Combs’ NYC concert back in the summer of 2024, and the video went viral on TikTok.

As Powell mentions, he got a taste of the country music life putting together the Twisters movie soundtrack, which hit no. 3 on the Billboard country album charts that summer, with Luke Combs’ “Ain’t No Love In Oklahoma” spending 15 weeks on the Billboard Hot 100.

A tale as old as Rocky, if you want a part in a specific film, write it yourself. According to Rolling Stone, Producer Kevin Misher connected Powell with Apatow shortly after the idea for The Comeback King was born, and the Scream Queens actor and the mind behind Knocked Up wrote the script together. This will be Apatow’s first directorial feature film since The Bubble (2022) and The King of Staten Island (2020).

In a recent development, I’m already sold on The Comeback King from the trailer alone. It’s got hilarious roasts, a redemption arc, and a ton of heart, all the hallmarks of a great Judd Apatow film. In The Comeback King, we see Glen Powell live out his wildest “beer for breakfast” fantasies (a nod to Luke Combs “Don’t Tempt Me”), until it all comes crashing down after his pop star girlfriend (Madelyn Cline) cheats and ruins his reputation. King then returns to his old college where his career all started, for redemption and maybe a latest shot at love. Check out the trailer below, and see if you can name the insane number of country music cameos:.

In a recent development, how Glen Powell was able to once again assemble the Avengers of country music, I’ll never know. But I’m super excited to see the likes of Miranda Lambert, Jelly Roll, Brad Paisley, and Shaboozey bring their A-game alongside Powell in this epic ensemble comedy when it premieres on February 5, 2027. While we wait for that, I think we should all say thank you to Luke Combs too for helping inspire this film that looks like it'll be a lot of country fun.

#97167. Tech Report: 10 Best Directing Duos Of All Time, Ranked

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2690 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashfilm ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: 10 Best Directing Duos Of All Time, Ranked

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
  • Recent findings suggest that most films treat the idea of the "director" with a dignified sense of reverence, especially since the end of the studio system.
  • While we've talked plenty about the medium's great moviemakers — indeed, we already have a list of the 25 best directors of all time — it seemed appropriate to carve out space for the history's great directing partnerships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Recent findings suggest that most films treat the idea of the "director" with a dignified sense of reverence, especially since the end of the studio system. Where the producer's role was once seen as paramount in getting a film made and even in achieving a certain artistic vision, a film's achievements are now often attributed to the isolated decisions of the all-vital director.

While we've talked plenty about the medium's great moviemakers — indeed, we already have a list of the 25 best directors of all time — it seemed appropriate to carve out space for the history's great directing partnerships. Though plenty of movies have two directors, the sustained union of two filmmakers over many years and/or films is rarer, and it warrants a closer look at the best of those recurring or long-lasting alliances. While the idea of the director usually implies one voice making the final decisions for the myriad creative components of a finished film, these directing duos prove that continuing that sense of collaboration into the chief position on a film set can bear rewarding fruit.

Here are the best directing duos of all time, ranked.

It has been revealed that jean-Pierre Jeunet and Marc Caro spent years honing their singular aesthetic in short films before making their feature debut with "Delicatessen," a pitch-black comedy set in a post-apocalyptic apartment building where a butcher-landlord keeps his tenants fed by turning unsuspecting newcomers into meat. Jeunet and Caro's penchant for grotesque faces and sickly yellow lighting helped make the film a sensation, earning it four César Awards, including Best First Film and Best Original or Adapted Screenplay.

Industry observers note that "The City of Lost Children" saw them double down on their peculiar sensibility: a fable set in a decaying port city, where a prematurely aging scientist steals children's dreams and a gentle circus strongman, played by Ron Perlman, searches for his kidnapped little brother. Its macabre, nightmarish storybook whimsy remains one of the most singular visions in French cinema — an underseen, visually stunning masterpiece.

Then the partnership abruptly ended. Jeunet was tapped to direct "Alien Resurrection", and his subsequent films, most famously the candy-colored "Amélie," have generally been warmer and more polished. Meanwhile, Caro's lone solo feature, the sci-fi film "Dante 01," never found the same audience. It makes for a fascinating what-if, as nobody has quite matched the blend of cruelty and tenderness the two cooked up together, and it's hard not to suspect that the grime and the heart needed each other.

John Musker and Ron Clements met at Disney while working on "The Fox and the Hound," and they went on to become one of the studio's most dependable directing teams during its biggest creative revival. They made their feature-directing debut alongside Burny Mattinson and David Michener on 1986's "The Great Mouse Detective," a Sherlock Holmes riff about a sleuthing rodent, before Clements pitched an adaptation of Hans Christian Andersen's "The Little Mermaid." Working with songwriters Howard Ashman and Alan Menken, they delivered a film that won Oscars for its score and for "Under the Sea" and helped kick off the Disney Renaissance.

It has been revealed that "Aladdin" followed in 1992. The now-iconic musical was the highest-grossing film of its year and the highest-grossing animated film to that point, earning two more Oscars for Menken's score and "A Whole Fresh World." The duo kept working through shifting tastes, with "Hercules" in 1997 and the sci-fi swashbuckler "Treasure Planet" in 2002, which flopped but has since found its defenders. They returned to hand-drawn animation with "The Princess and the Frog" in 2009, then made their first fully computer-animated feature with "Moana," which earned an Oscar nomination for Best Animated Feature. It also spawned a widely criticized, remarkably premature live-action remake — part of a trend the pair described as "bemusing.".

Recent findings suggest that the pair has since retired, closing out a partnership that lasted more than three decades. Their films were defined by the fundamentals of Disney magic: musical numbers that developed the plot and emotions, and humor that never smothered the pathos underneath. Few directors have made so many movies that feel so effortlessly designed for all audiences.

According to recent reports, before they set box-office records, Joe and Anthony Russo were comedy filmmakers from Cleveland. After their micro-budget debut, "Pieces", Steven Soderbergh and George Clooney produced their second feature, "Welcome to Collinwood." The brothers broke through on television, winning an Emmy for directing the pilot of "Arrested Development," then directing the pilot of "Community" and many beloved episodes after it.

Sources indicate that that sitcom background is key to the work that followed in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, where their instincts for staging a dozen characters trading blows and punchlines helped define the quippy, ensemble-driven sensibility of their "Avengers" movies. However, that style has become a grievance among certain viewers who wish the films could escape their unrelenting sense of brand management. The brothers have cited François Truffaut and the French Newly introduced Wave as major influences, but their biggest films operate within decidedly conventional blockbuster boundaries. Still, there's no denying the level of control needed to orchestrate some of the biggest hits of the 2010s.

Sources indicate that their post-Marvel streaming films, including "Cherry," "The Gray Man," and "The Electric State," have been considerably less successful creatively. But through their company AGBO, they also produced the far more inventive "Everything Everywhere All at Once." With "Avengers: Doomsday" scheduled for December 2026, the brothers are once again tasked with herding Hollywood's biggest cast into something halfway coherent — a feat they've proven capable of, against all odds.

Recent findings suggest that justin Benson and Aaron Moorhead work on the principle that a tiny budget and a big idea can take you a long way. They broke out with "Resolution," which premiered at Tribeca in 2012, a lo-fi two-hander about a man who holes up in a remote cabin with his drug-addicted friend while something strange lurks beyond the walls. "Spring" followed in 2014, a Lovecraftian romance set on the Italian coast that fuses monster spectacle with the heart of a character drama. Benson typically writes and Moorhead handles cinematography, but the two co-direct and often appear on screen.

According to recent reports, that approach led to "The Endless," in which they play brothers returning to the cult they escaped. The film explicitly connects to "Resolution", establishing a shared cosmic-horror mythology. "Synchronic," their 2019 time-bending drug thriller with Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan, contains looser connections to that world, while the pandemic-era "Something in the Dirt" finds them starring as neighbors chasing a supernatural mystery.

Marvel took notice. They directed episodes of "Moon Knight" and much of the second season of "Loki," then helped rework the first season of "Daredevil: Born Again" before returning for its second. You could have worse pairs acting as custodians for one of the entertainment industry's biggest brands. Even if their Marvel work lacks the more personal flourishes of their smaller projects, you can still feel their indie-horror sensibility breaking through.

Industry observers note that daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert met at Emerson College and built their reputation on music videos, most famously DJ Snake and Lil Jon's "Turn Down for What", before making their feature debut with "Swiss Army Man," an emotionally vulnerable absurdist comedy about Paul Dano befriending a flatulent corpse played by Daniel Radcliffe. The movie's surprisingly tender treatment of shame, loneliness, and the weird stuff that makes us human earned the duo the U.S. Dramatic Directing Award at Sundance in 2016.

In a recent development, that set the stage for their true breakout: "Everything Everywhere All at Once" cranked their style to maximalist levels in one of the decade's most unexpected hits. Michelle Yeoh's exhausted laundromat owner is dragged across the multiverse in a hyper-stylized, daffy yet sincere family drama about an immigrant mother and her daughter facing the potential end of the world. It was A24's highest-grossing release at the time — the studio's first film to reach $100 million worldwide — and won seven of its 11 Oscar nominations, including Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Original Screenplay, plus acting wins for Yeoh, Ke Huy Quan, and Jamie Lee Curtis.

Industry observers note that that made the Daniels only the third directing pair to win Best Director, after Robert Wise & Jerome Robbins and Joel & Ethan Coen. Though prone to hyperactivity, few other filmmakers could make a hot-dog-fingers gag and a mother-daughter reconciliation feel like parts of the same carefully calculated thematic throughline. Here's hoping their next film, with Matt Damon attached, sustains that momentum.

Recent findings suggest that phil Lord and Christopher Miller have built a career on finding inventiveness in projects that might have become franchise mediocrity under other filmmakers. The Dartmouth classmates started in television, co-creating the short-lived MTV cult satire "Clone High," before making their feature debut with "Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs," a frantic, silly adaptation of a children's picture book filled with surprisingly clever gags and character detail.

The duo kept pace: "21 Jump Street," a seemingly ill-conceived reboot of a 1980s TV drama as a buddy-cop farce, became one of the 2010s' most successful and acclaimed comedies. "The LEGO Movie," seemingly a feature-length branding exercise, became an inventive parable about creativity and conformity, launching a franchise of other LEGO films while transforming a bad premise into a cinematic miracle.

Their commitment to a distinct filmmaking voice also caused friction within the franchise machine, leading to their firing from "Solo: A Star Wars Story" late in production, though they went on to find other successes. As producers of "Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse," they helped push the possibilities of mainstream animation forward. They also drew on their "Star Wars" experience in making 2026's "Project Hail Mary," a funny, meticulously crafted, heart-on-its-sleeve adaptation of Andy Weir's novel that has grossed roughly $685 million worldwide. The pair's irreverence remains central to their success: tongue-in-cheek self-awareness and a genuine love of subverting expectations have helped them turn unlikely premises into crowd-pleasers.

Lana and Lilly Wachowski came out of Chicago as comic-book obsessives, finding work as screenwriters before announcing themselves as directors with "Bound," a lean, sultry neo-noir starring Jennifer Tilly and Gina Gershon that showed off their formal command on a small budget. Then came "The Matrix," the iconic 1999 sci-fi smash that fused Hong Kong martial arts, anime, and heady cyberpunk philosophy into a defining text of 2000s action cinema. Its "bullet time" effects were imitated endlessly; it broke box-office records, and cinema was never quite the same.

But what really sets the sisters apart is how stubbornly they kept betting massive. "Speed Racer" may have flopped on release, but it has since gained recognition as a forward-thinking work of art. Similarly, "Cloud Atlas" and "Sense8," their Netflix series about psychically linked strangers, have attracted devoted defenders of the Wachowskis' uncompromising vision. Even "Jupiter Ascending" has its champions. Their work has also invited a deeper reading of "The Matrix" as a trans allegory, something Lilly has discussed directly.

The sisters have pursued separate projects in recent years. Lana directed 2021's caustically self-referential "The Matrix Resurrections" on her own, while Lilly has been developing "The Hunted," a mid-sized thriller with an all-transgender cast. Even while working apart, both continue to follow the amplified, philosophical sensibilities that made their collaborations so distinctive.

Widely known as engineers of feature-length anxiety attacks, Josh and Benny Safdie were among the most exciting filmmakers working in New York before their broader breakthrough. They first drew attention with "Daddy Longlegs," a scrappy, semi-autobiographical portrait of a chaotic father that played Cannes' Directors' Fortnight in 2009. Then came "Heaven Knows What," a bruising drama about people struggling with heroin addiction, starring Arielle Holmes and drawn from her own experiences and writings. Their method of handheld close-ups, overlapping dialogue, and nonprofessionals cast alongside movie stars came together in "Good Time," in which Robert Pattinson plays a small-time crook losing control of one long night.

The apex was "Uncut Gems," in which Adam Sandler gave a career-defining performance as a gambling-addicted Diamond District jeweler hurtling through two hours of escalating bad decisions — a stress-riddled, darkly funny drama of street-level chaos and apprehension.

The brothers have since pursued separate directing careers, and differences in their sensibilities emerged in their solo work. Benny's "The Smashing Machine," with Dwayne Johnson as MMA fighter Mark Kerr, struggled commercially but revealed a quieter, more observant side of his filmmaking. Josh's "Marty Supreme," with Timothée Chalamet as a force of chaos, continued the streak of relentless havoc. Both films still carry the fingerprints of what the two built together: textured environments, tightly observed characters, and an acute sense of the worlds they inhabit. But the partnership that produced "Uncut Gems" remains one of the most electrifying of its era.

Recent findings suggest that few partnerships have been as productive or as generous to film history as Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger. Although Powell generally handled on-set direction and Pressburger originated many of their stories, they famously shared writing, producing, and directing credit during their peak years as the Archers. Powell, an Englishman who learned his craft on British quota quickies, and Pressburger, a Hungarian screenwriter who fled Nazi Germany, first teamed up in 1939. Pressburger later won an Oscar for the original story of 1941's "49th Parallel," and in the early 1940s they formed their production manufacturer, the Archers, whose films opened with an arrow striking a target.

That led to one of the great runs in British cinema: the wartime satire "The Life and Death of Colonel Blimp," the pastoral "A Canterbury Tale," the romance "I Know Where I'm Going!," and "A Matter of Life and Death," a fantasy about a pilot who cheats death. "Black Narcissus" won Oscars for Jack Cardiff's cinematography and Alfred Junge's art direction, while "The Red Shoes" remains an utterly dazzling film about artistic obsession, with its nearly 17-minute ballet sequence nestled inside a classical yet fantastical melodrama.

Their main partnership ended after 1957's "Ill Met by Moonlight," though they collaborated again on smaller projects, including "They're a Weird Mob" and "The Boy Who Turned Yellow." Powell's solo thriller "Peeping Tom" was so reviled by British critics that it badly damaged his career, though it has since been rediscovered as a masterpiece, thanks in no small part to Martin Scorsese.

Industry observers note that joel and Ethan Coen have long worked like one filmmaker with two heads, though Directors Guild rules obscured that for two decades by crediting Joel as director and Ethan as producer. The two also shared editing duties under the pseudonym Roderick Jaynes, a nonexistent editor who nonetheless earned Oscar nominations for "Fargo" and "No Country for Old Men." They finally received joint directing credit with 2004's "The Ladykillers." By then, the work had long spoken for itself: "Blood Simple" and "Raising Arizona" confirmed a pair of formalists with a wicked sense of humor, and "Barton Fink" swept Cannes in 1991.

It has been revealed that working frequently with cinematographer Roger Deakins, they moved between screwball comedy ("Raising Arizona," "Burn After Reading"), gangster pictures ("Miller's Crossing"), and Westerns ("True Grit") with unmatched formal and tonal precision. Few filmmakers could make movies as equally iconic as "The Substantial Lebowski" and "No Country for Old Men," works at opposite ends of the tonal spectrum that still feel unmistakably of a piece with the brothers' sardonic, philosophical sensibility.

Recent findings suggest that after 2018's "The Ballad of Buster Scruggs," the brothers pursued solo directing projects, with Joel making "The Tragedy of Macbeth" and Ethan making "Drive-Away Dolls" and "Honey Don't!" But in October 2026, while receiving the Lumière Prize in Lyon, they said they planned to direct another film together. Joel's upcoming "Jack of Spades," which Ethan co-wrote and Netflix intends to release theatrically in fall 2027, is still a solo directing project, but their reunion comments suggest another collaboration may be ahead. Hopefully they'll add another movie to a remarkable joint filmography, which we've ranked in full.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • November 2, 1947: Queen Elizabeth—then Princess Elizabeth—with Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, King George VI and Queen Elizabeth (right) and members of the immediate and extended Royal Family at Buckingham Palace after their wedding.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip married in 1947, going on to make history by achieving the longest marriage of any British sovereign couple. Back then they were, of course, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, tying the knot in the rather austere years of post-war Britain. So, what really happened on their wedding day?

November 2, 1947: Queen Elizabeth—then Princess Elizabeth—with Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, King George VI and Queen Elizabeth (right) and members of the immediate and extended Royal Family at Buckingham Palace after their wedding.

Sources indicate that the Queen and Prince Philip’s love story began back in 1939. Princess Elizabeth was just 13 years old; her dashing distant cousin, Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, was five years her senior and about to join the Royal Navy. They met as she toured the Royal Naval College at Dartmouth; he was the young officer assigned to escort her around that day.

Determined to marry for love, Elizabeth was said to be rather taken with Philip, who was described at the time as ‘handsome as any film star.’ The pair were soon writing letters to each other, and later, occasional chaperoned meetings took place.

The couple on their engagement, 1947.

In a recent development, in 1946 Philip proposed in Scotland, and she immediately remarked yes. However, her father, King George, reportedly insisted the couple resist announcing their engagement until the Princess, who was just 20, was a little older. In the end, her parents gave in to her wishes, and Philip officially proposed to Princess Elizabeth in 1947, with a three-carat diamond ring he designed using stones taken from a family tiara that belonged to his mother, Princess Alice of Battenberg. It was created by London jeweller Philip Antrobus Ltd.

Princess Elizabeth with Philip Mountbatten on their wedding day.

The Royal Family were adamant that the wedding of Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip would reflect the country’s post-war situation while also offering a chance for the nation to celebrate.

Like many brides at the time, Princess Elizabeth had to save her rationing coupons to buy the materials for her dress but was given an extra 200 from the government to help. While well-wishers generously sent their own to the royal, they had to be sent back as rules dictated that coupons could not be shared outside of households.

Recent findings suggest that designed by Norman Hartnell, Princess Elizabeth’s wedding dress was made from ivory silk, duchesse satin and silver thread; the dress featured crystals, 10,000 seed pearls, a fitted bodice, heart-shaped neckline, long sleeves and a 15-foot train. It was made in just seven weeks by 350 skilled women since the wedding took place only four months after the couple’s engagement announcement. Norman Hartnell also designed Elizabeth’s going-away outfit.

Industry observers note that princess Elizabeth’s wedding day tiara was called the Queen Mary Fringe Tiara. It had belonged to her grandmother, Queen Mary, and had been given to her as a wedding present in 1893. It was remade from a tiara/necklace that Queen Victoria had bought from Collingwood and Co.

Industry observers note that as Elizabeth was getting ready on the morning of the wedding, it snapped. Luckily, royal jeweler Garrard was apparently on hand to fix it, and the Queen later revealed, “I think he taped up the spring.”.

In a recent development, princess Elizabeth’s other wedding day jewelry included two pearl necklaces. The shorter of the two necklaces was the “Queen Anne” necklace, noted to have belonged to Anne, the last Stuart Queen. The other was known as the “Queen Caroline,” and is said to have belonged to the wife of King George II. Both necklaces were left to the Crown by Queen Victoria and were given to Elizabeth as a wedding present by her father.

Sources indicate that all royal bridal bouquets contain myrtle from a myrtle bush planted by Queen Victoria at Osborne House. Princess Elizabeth’s also had white orchids and was laid on the grave of the Unknown Warrior at Westminster Abbey the day after the wedding.

There were eight bridesmaids at Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip’s wedding: Princess Margaret, Princess Alexandra, Lady Pamela Mountbatten, Diana Bowes-Lyon, Lady Elizabeth Lambart, Margaret Elphinstone, Lady Caroline Montagu-Douglas-Scott, and Lady Mary Cambridge.

Her two pages were Prince William of Gloucester and Prince Michael of Kent, both aged five at the time.

The bridesmaids were given silver Art Deco-style compacts with the couple's initials and a crown engraved on the lid, set with five cabochon sapphires.

The Duke of Edinburgh's best man was David Mountbatten, the Marquess of Milford Haven.

Knowing that Elizabeth hated cigarettes, Prince Philip reportedly gave up smoking on the morning of his wedding “suddenly and apparently without difficulty,” according to his valet, John Dean.

According to recent reports, the wedding took place at Westminster Abbey on November, 20th, 1947 at 11:30 a.m. Princess Elizabeth was the 10th member of the Royal Family to be married at Westminster Abbey.

Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip walking down the aisle of Westminster Abbey, followed by their bridesmaids and pages.

There were 2,000 guests in attendance, including the likes of the King of Iraq, Princess Juliana and Prince Bernhard of the Netherlands and the Hereditary Grand Duke of Luxembourg and Princess Elisabeth of Luxembourg. The ceremony was broadcast on the radio to millions of listeners.

In a recent development, together with her father, Princess Elizabeth left Buckingham Palace in the Irish State Coach. (In her later years, it had been Queen Victoria’s state carriage of choice, as she declined to use the Gold State Coach following the death of Prince Albert.).

The wedding ceremony was officiated by the Archbishop of Canterbury, Geoffrey Fisher, and the Archbishop of York, Cyril Garbett.

The organist and Master of the Choristers at the Abbey, Australian William Neil McKie, was the director of music for the wedding and there were 91 singers; the abbey choir was joined by the choirs of the Chapel Royal and St George's Chapel in Windsor.

The service started with a specially composed fanfare by Arnold Bax and finished with Felix Mendelssohn's “Wedding March,” with ceremony hymns including “Praise, my Soul, the King of Heaven” and “The Lord's my Shepherd.”.

The bride and groom knelt on orange boxes covered in pink silk at the altar as a nod to post-war austerity.

In a recent development, on the day of the wedding, Philip was given the title of Duke of Edinburgh by his father-in-law, King George VI. After the Queen ascended the throne in 1953, she made the decision in 1957 to make Philip a prince of the UK, in addition to his dukedom.

The wedding rings were made from a nugget of Welsh gold which came from the Clogau St David's mine, near Dolgellau.

According to Royal biographer Ingrid Seward, who wrote Prince Philip: Revealed, Philip had a secret message inscribed inside his wife's wedding band, a message that only the engraver, Queen Elizabeth, and her husband knew the contents of.

After the service, a wedding breakfast was held in the Ball-Supper Room at Buckingham Palace for 150 guests only, with Filet de Sole Mountbatten, Perdreau en Casserole and Bombe Glacée Princess Elizabeth on the menu.

During the breakfast, the string band of the Grenadier Guards played music while guests were greeted with individual posies of myrtle and white Balmoral on their place settings as the wedding favors.

The couple waving from the balcony of Buckingham Palace.

Famously, the newlyweds went onto the balcony at Buckingham Palace to wave to the huge crowds on the Mall.

Although the royal couple received 11 wedding cakes, the official traditional fruit cake was baked by McVitie and Price and was four tiers and nine feet high. The wedding cake was decorated with both coats of arms, including the monograms of the bride and groom, sugar-iced figures of their favorite activities, and regimental and naval badges.

Mr Schur, chief confectioner at McVitie and Price, putting the final touches to the wedding cake.

The newlyweds cut the cake using the Duke's Mountbatten sword, which was a wedding present from the King.

Recent findings suggest that over 10,000 people sent telegrams congratulating Elizabeth and Philip, and around 2,500 wedding presents were sent from around the world. These included a cloth from Mahatma Gandhi that he’d woven himself, which Queen Mary mistook for an “indelicate” loincloth.

After their wedding breakfast, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip headed to Waterloo station, joined by Elizabeth’s corgi, Susan, catching a train to Hampshire to spend their wedding night in Broadlands, the home of Philip's uncle, Earl Mountbatten.

The rest of their royal honeymoon was spent at Birkhall on the Balmoral Estate in Scotland.

Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip being showered with rose petals as they leave Buckingham Palace, London, for their honeymoon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that roger Ebert wasn't as effusive about Peter Jackson's "The Lord of the Rings" films as many other critics. For reference, Ebert gave "Fellowship of the Ring" and "The Two Towers" three stars (out of four) and then "Return of the King" three and a half.

According to recent reports, "A true visualization of [J.R.R.] Tolkien's Middle-earth it is not," wrote Ebert of Jackson's "Fellowship," arguing it "adds up to more of a sword and sorcery epic" that loses the "innocence" of the books. Though, Ebert conceded in that review that "That 'Fellowship of the Ring' doesn't match my imaginary vision of Middle-earth is my problem, not yours.".

Ebert subsequently wrote that the action of "The Two Towers" "would no doubt startle the gentle medievalist J.R.R. Tolkien." However, he praised "Return of the King" as a strong conclusion which solidified the trilogy as "a work of bold ambition at a time of cinematic timidity," even if he felt the film and trilogy fell "a little shy of greatness.".

But you know what fantasy movie Ebert did love? 2007's "The Golden Compass," adapted from Philip Pullman's "His Dark Materials" novels. It's set in an alternate world where a piece of every person's soul exists in the form of an animal, called a dæmon. British orphan Lyra Belacqua (Dakota Blue Richards) embarks on a quest to rescue a friend and stumbles onto a much more cosmic struggle. Ebert gave it four stars, writing:.

"'The Golden Compass' is a darker, deeper fantasy epic than the 'Rings' trilogy, 'The Chronicles of Narnia' or the 'Potter' films. It springs from the same British world of quasi-philosophical magic, but creates more complex villains and poses more intriguing questions.".

While most would disagree with Ebert's quality assessment, he's onto something, as "Golden Compass" invites "Lord of the Rings" comparisons.

"The Golden Compass" was produced by Fresh Line Cinema, the same production tech giant behind "The Lord of the Rings," and it's clear the studio was hoping to repeat its previous success. "The Golden Compass" even features two key "Rings" alums: Ian McKellen (Gandalf) as the voice of polar bear king Iorek Byrnison, and Christopher Lee (the corrupted wizard Saruman) as a leader of the Magisterium, the Church of Lyra's world. It was reported in 2007 both actors were cast at New Line's behest.

But quite the contrary, "The Golden Compass" under-performed ($372 million in theaters against a $180 million budget), and sequels were never made. "The Golden Compass" even contributed to the end of New Line as an independent studio, as it was folded into Warner Bros. in 2008. Not helping the movie's financials was a religious backlash. The Magisterium allegorically represents all authoritarian religions but especially the Catholic Church, and "The Golden Compass" was in turn condemned by the Vatican.

"The Golden Compass" didn't win over fans of its source novel, either, due to abundant changes. The movie cuts out the book's entire ending, which directly sets up the sequel, "The Subtle Knife." But the attacks on religion? Those are taken right from the book. Philip Pullman is an atheist, and "His Dark Materials" is his rebuttal to the Christian-themed British fantasies of J.R.R. Tolkien and "Chronicles of Narnia" author C.S. Lewis, particularly the latter as both stories are about children traveling to different worlds. (Though Tolkien, for what it's worth, is mentioned to have disliked "Narnia.").

Industry observers note that "I cordially dislike allegory," Tolkien once famously claimed, believing it robs readers the freedom to interpret a work. For decades, stated readers have since read into the influence of Tolkien's Catholic faith on his Middle-earth stories.

In a recent development, sauron and his ring are a Luciferian conception of evil: A fallen angel who rules a fiery, molten realm and whose darkness spreads as temptation. J. R. R. Tolkien's villain is the Devil, Philip Pullman's is the Church.

According to recent reports, frodo carrying the ring echoes Christ carrying his own cross to Golgotha and, in turn, the metaphorical crosses that all of Christ's followers carry. "The Chronicles of Narnia," meanwhile, features talking lion Aslan as a direct allegory for the Christian God, Christ-like sacrifice and resurrection included.

In "His Dark Materials," the Magisterium worships "the Authority," a name suggesting an "authority" is all that organized religion is. The Authority is also a liar: He is not the creator of the universe, merely the first "angel" who came into being. The weak and withered "god" eventually crumbles into dust, as if humanity has no more use for him. The very last dialogue of the trilogy is Lyra endeavoring to build a "Republic of Heaven" on Earth.

Yet, circling back to Roger Ebert, he disputed the anti-religious reading of the "Golden Compass" movie, arguing it reworks the Magisterium into a more purely political villain, "a Soviet dictatorship or Significant Brother." He specifically praised the film's themes as "murky," compared to Pullman's blatant allegory for the death of God, and affirmed that "the controversy surrounding ['The Golden Compass'] obscures its function as a splendid entertainment.".

Sources indicate that amusingly, Ebert championed the movie for the same reasons many "His Dark Materials" fans rejected it. Toning down the anti-religion elements did not spare the movie the Church's wrath, either. One can only wonder what Ebert would have thought of the eventual "His Dark Materials" TV series that adapted Pullman's story to book fans' delight.

Tech Report: Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a newly introduced filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the company complies.
  • As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct customers to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.
  • Apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a newly introduced filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the company complies. Here are the details.

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct customers to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

At the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a new filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its upcoming filing, Epic says Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the organization of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

According to recent reports, apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple states decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s newly introduced CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”.

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

Under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

It has been revealed that given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”.

According to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a fresh order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The 1966 psychological drama was made following a bout of severe illness for Bergman, during which he was struck by a vision of two women slowly merging into one identity.
  • Aside from urging viewers to feel rather than understand "Persona," Ingmar Bergman explained the film as a sonata for the instruments that were Bibi Andersson and Liv Ullmann.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you're tired of a mass culture that pumps out Harry Potter reboot series and Chris Pratt films so bad even AI couldn't generate them, why not revisit one of the great films of the 20th Century. Ingmar Bergman's "Persona" is currently available to watch on HBO Max, and offers a wonderfully confounding, disturbing yet lyrical experience that any film fan should see at least once. You're not going to have much of a clue about what's going on, but that's sort of the point.

The 1966 psychological drama was made following a bout of severe illness for Bergman, during which he was struck by a vision of two women slowly merging into one identity. "Persona" was the realization of that vision. It stars Liv Ullmann as an actress named Elisabet who during a stage performance suddenly stops speaking and moving. Her doctor advises she be taken to a remote seaside cottage to be nursed back to health. That job falls to nurse, Alma (Bibi Andersson) who in her frequent one-sided conversations with her mute patient reveals candid details of her own past. As their time together goes on, Alma and Elisabet begin to assume each other's identities.

Aside from urging viewers to feel rather than understand "Persona," Ingmar Bergman explained the film as a sonata for the instruments that were Bibi Andersson and Liv Ullmann. Andersson had worked with Bergman regularly since their first collaboration on "Smiles of a Summer Night" in 1955. "Persona" was, however, Norwegian actress Liv Ullmann's first Bergman film. Given the director's view of it as a "sonata" for the pair, it would seem the filmmaker was interested in his actors more than anything else.

But "Persona" is full of fascinating symbolism and is thematically rich enough that it's spawned endless critical analysis interpreting the film as everything from a modernist horror movie to an interrogation of acting itself as an art form. It's also been interpreted as an exploration of the distinction between our true selves and the masks we wear in social settings — which, considering the film's title, clearly has some relevance.

Sources indicate that but even Roger Ebert admitted to not understanding the movie upon his initial viewing in 1967. When the critic revisited "Persona" in 2001, he still seemed somewhat perplexed, even while writing, "I know most of what I am ever likely to know about films, and I think I understand that the best approach to 'Persona' is a literal one." The ending of "Persona" certainly offers no answers, but it's not supposed to. Susan Sontag wrote that "Persona" is "bound to trouble, perplex and frustrate most filmgoers," and it does — but in the most beautiful, mesmeric, and disturbing way possible. The film is streaming on HBO Max at the time of writing, but can also be found on the usual digital platforms as well as on archive.org for free.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As detailed by AppleInsider, a latest Morgan Stanley research report claims Apple is poised to ship approximately 270 million iPhones in 2027, a 7% bump from 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that apple could see iPhone shipments rise 7% next year, giving it a 26% share of global smartphone shipments, according to a newly introduced report. Here are the details.

As detailed by AppleInsider, a latest Morgan Stanley research report claims Apple is poised to ship approximately 270 million iPhones in 2027, a 7% bump from 2026.

The forecast comes amid a change of pace for Apple, which released only the iPhone 18 Pro models and iPhone Duo this fall, with the rest of its iPhone lineup reportedly set to arrive early next year.

Morgan Stanley notes that this could push some purchases from late 2026 into 2027, contributing to the projected shipment growth without necessarily reflecting an increase in underlying demand.

The report also comes as Apple and the rest of the smartphone industry continue to grapple with rising memory and storage prices, though previous reports have suggested that Apple is better positioned than many of its competitors to absorb those costs.

Apple raised iPhone prices in September, after keeping them stable for much of the year while competitors had already introduced price hikes. In some cases, they raised prices more than once within a matter of months.

Back to the report, it notes that global smartphone shipments are expected to drop 5% next year, compared with a previous forecast of 3.6% growth. That mentioned, it’s still an improvement over the estimated 13.8% decline in 2026.

In a recent development, when it comes to Apple and the iPhone specifically, Morgan Stanley notes that consumer interest in upgrading has remained largely unchanged year over year, with 37% of iPhone owners saying they are extremely likely to upgrade within the next 12 months. That’s compared with 41% of smartphone owners overall, a figure that dropped by 2 percentage points year over year.

As for the market’s reaction to the iPhone Duo, Morgan Stanley found that 22% of non-iPhone owners surveyed expressed interest in switching to Apple’s foldable device, with that figure reaching 34% in China.

Importantly, Morgan Stanley’s survey was conducted after the iPhone Duo was announced, but before it introduced, so these figures reflect consumer interest rather than actual purchasing behavior.

Apple Intelligence was another factor examined in the survey, with Morgan Stanley concluding that AI features are becoming less key in driving iPhone upgrades, while factors such as battery life and upgrade eligibility are gaining importance.

Finally, Morgan Stanley found that Apple’s customer retention rate increased three percentage points to a record 93%, while its net switching rate improved to 12%.

Huawei was the only other major smartphone brand to show a positive and improving net switching rate, while Samsung and Google remained relatively neutral, and Xiaomi, Motorola, Honor, Oppo, and Vivo recorded negative rates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since the beginning of the week, the James Bond frenzy has shown no signs of stopping. On November 16, upcoming Bond owners Amazon MGM Studios finally revealed the name of the actor who will succeed Daniel Craig as 007: Robert Pattinson. After years of speculation and months of intense rumors, the next James Bond now has a new face. Now, the next question on everyone’s mind: Who will be the next Bond girl?

The exception in thie great debate is Léa Seydoux. The actor, who seems to be everywhere this year, played Madeleine Swann in Craig's final Bond films, Spectre (2015) and No Time to Die (2021). Her magnetic performance made Madeleine an unforgettable Bond girl, especially since her character plays a decisive role in the arc of Craig’s character: at the end of No Time to Die, the famous spy sacrifices himself to save her and their daughter, Mathilde. For the first time since its creation in 1953 by British author Ian Fleming, the secret agent in Her Majesty’s service was gone.

Léa Seydoux and Daniel Craig pose as they arrive on the set of No Time To Die on September 09, 2019 in Matera, Italy.

In a recent interview on Vogue's The Run-Through podcast, Seydoux was candid about how little interest she had in her successor. “I don’t really care,” she said with a laugh. “I don’t really care, guys. How can you?”.

When pressed on who Pattinson's female lead might be, Seydoux expressed mixed feelings about the British spy's latest iteration. With the purchase of the Bond IP by Amazon, “It became American," Seydoux noted. “But I’m sure the movie will be great because it’s directed by Denis Villeneuve, who’s a very talented director. I’m sure he will do something great.”.

The online megamart took control of the storied franchise in 2023, after which Amazon founder Jeff Bezos controversially sought feedback on the title character's casting via X. The announcement of Villeneuve as the next film's director brought things back from the brink.

Industry observers note that bezos, who confirmed that he was “very involved” in the film's casting process, also seems to give Seydoux pause. In an interview with Variety, she admitted “was a bit sad when I heard that it was sold (…) but now that it’s Denis, I was like, Oh, at least it’s him, so it will be cinema.”.

It has been revealed that denis Villeneuve, who directed Seydoux in Dune: Part Two, will release the final installment of this epic science-fiction trilogy will be on December 16. After that, he'll be free to focus on his next major project: reviving the world’s most famous secret agent. It remains to be seen who he will choose to star opposite Robert Pattinson as his female companion—but we know that despite her fondness for the director, Seydoux will not return: Just last month, the French actress told People “I really loved being on this franchise, but now it’s ... done.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Mists are apparently rolling into Netflix.

Sources indicate that A live-action Dungeons & Dragons series based on Ravenloft is in development at Netflix, giving the tabletop gaming franchise’s most famous horror setting its own shot at TV. The project, simply titled Ravenloft, comes from screenwriter John August, Alfonso Cuarón, and Hasbro Entertainment, and is described as the successor to Netflix's other, now-canceled D&D project, The Forgotten Realms.

While Dungeons & Dragons is often associated with taverns, dragons, treasure, and quippy adventuring parties, Ravenloft is the game’s gothic nightmare corner. It’s the place where D&D trades high-fantasy heroics for haunted castles, cursed lands, tragic monsters and the sense that there's always something lurking in the fog.

Ravenloft has been one of D&D’s most iconic settings for decades, dating back to the original 1983 adventure built around Count Strahd von Zarovich. Strahd remains the setting’s defining villain — he's a vampire lord, tragic monster, and tyrant trapped in the mist-shrouded land of Barovia.

Recent findings suggest that the setting later grew into the Domains of Dread, a collection of horror realms ruled by Darklords who are often imprisoned in worlds shaped by their own sins and obsessions. The premise gives the TV show a lot of flexibility in the stories it tells, bouncing between gothic horrors, cursed folklore, and actual nightmares within the one setting.

Industry observers note that that flexibility is a big part of why Ravenloft has endured. While Curse of Strahd remains the best-known modern entry point for many D&D players, newer books like Van Richten’s Guide to Ravenloft and Ravenloft: The Horrors Within have expanded the setting beyond Barovia, turning it into a toolkit for nearly every flavor of horror D&D can support.

Recent findings suggest that according to a Deadline report, the Ravenloft project is also part of a broader push to expand D&D outside the core tabletop game. Netflix had also been developing The Forgotten Realms, though Deadline reports Ravenloft is now positioned as its successor. Meanwhile, a sequel to Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves remains uncertain, even though co-writer and co-director Jonathan Goldstein recently mentioned a script exists.

According to recent reports, D&D’s reach has also been boosted by projects that don’t look like traditional tabletop products. People are still playing, modding and arguing about Baldur’s Gate 3 years after its 2023 launch, while Critical Role has helped turn actual play into a major entertainment lane of its own, with live indicates, animated adaptations, and a huge audience beyond the table.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud. Here are the details.

A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.

At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid looks for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.

Now, the site reports that some WhatsApp people running the latest TestFlight build are seeing the option to switch from iCloud to WhatsApp’s own backup service, suggesting that a wider rollout may not be too far off.

Industry observers note that customers can switch to WhatsApp cloud storage from the Chat backup screen. Here, users will have to choose the backup provider they want to use. If they choose WhatsApp, they will have to secure their backups using end-to-end encryption. Since encryption is mandatory, users cannot skip this step. However, they can choose a different method to encrypt their backups. For example, users can secure their backups using a 64-digit encryption key. Users who do not know what to choose can opt for the passkey, which is the default method WhatsApp recommends. After users complete the setup, they can back up their chat history on WhatsApp’s servers. WhatsApp keeps the backup on its servers for four months after a subscription expires. If users do not renew their subscription, WhatsApp deletes the backup permanently.

Importantly, the site notes that backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers cannot currently be used to restore chats across platforms, meaning people switching from iPhone to Android, or vice versa, will still need to rely on WhatsApp’s built-in chat transfer feature.

Although the feature appears to be rolling out to beta testers first, the report notes that “the latest version available on the App Store is also compatible with this functionality,” meaning WhatsApp could theoretically enable it for users running the public version without requiring another app revision.
