💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing.
  • It has been revealed that “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire.
  • Industry observers note that the lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be vital for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

It has been revealed that “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”.

Industry observers note that the lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be vital for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

It has been revealed that “When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was important to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado stated. “.

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

According to recent reports, for Crawford, the significant lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

According to recent reports, “The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”.

In a recent development, still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

“Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado said. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”.

Sources indicate that this all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford remarked, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other massive studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

The legendary science fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke once noted, “Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.” The lines between sci-fi and fantasy blur in popular entertainment franchises like Star Wars, Warhammer 40,000, and the Marvel Cinematic Universe, as well as in classic book series like Dune and Dragonriders of Pern. If you’re looking for a new world to explore and can’t decide if you want it filled with spaceships or dragons, you don’t necessarily have to choose. Just pick something from this list of the best science fantasy books of the 21st century.

It has been revealed that marissa Meyer’s debut novel puts a science fiction spin on the tale of Cinderella. A cyborg mechanic living in New Beijing, Cinder discovers a royal conspiracy involving the denizens of the Moon, who have the ability to manipulate people by controlling their bioelectricity. Cinder kicked off Meyer’s long-running The Lunar Chronicles series, which is being adapted into an animated TV show. Other books continue the series’ blend of science fiction and fairy tales, incorporating satellites, genetic engineering, and spaceships into retellings of Rapunzel, Little Red Riding Hood, and Snow White.​​​​​​​.

N. K. Jemisin’s Hugo Award-winning novel ​​​​​​​is extremely bleak: it opens with the world’s destruction and follows three women as they deal with the aftermath.​​​​​​​ The first book in the Broken Earth series explores the devastating effects of climate change and intolerance, as people with the same sort of power that shattered the world have to hide their abilities for fear of being killed by angry mobs or their own families. In classic Clarke fashion, what seems to be magic turns out to be tied to forgotten technology.​​​​​​​.

In a recent development, charlie Jane Anders' Nebula Award-winning book celebrates all sorts of weird kids by following the relationship between Patricia, a young witch, and Laurence, a boy genius who invents his own time machine. Fantasy and science fiction stories regularly deal with apocalyptic threats, but this world is unraveling slowly due to war and devastating storms. Patricia and Laurence come together and grow apart several times over the course of their lives, but their love might hold the key to bringing magic and science together and saving humanity.

The first book in the Machineries of Empire trilogy follows Kel Cheris, a soldier tasked with retaking a fortress captured by heretical enemies of the galactic government. ​​​​​​​To retake the fortress, Cheris must combine her consciousness with the mind of one of the greatest tacticians of all time.​​​​​​​ General Shuos Jedao was executed after killing a million people, including his own forces, using a devastating weapon. Cheris has to figure out how much she can trust Jedao and her own superiors toas she tries to complete the mission and stay alive. The space opera is infused with Korean folklore, blending science and magic through the concept of calendrical workings, where ritual observances fuel mind-control powers and technologies that break the laws of physics.

Nyr is actually an anthropologist from Earth sent to monitor an abandoned colony, and he isn’t supposed to get involved in local problems. This article contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

Prequel film "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" reveals the details of how Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada, Woody Harrelson in the original films) won the 50th Hunger Games ... and lost everything else in his life, turning him into a miserable man using alcohol to cope. Yet "The Hunger Games: Catching Fire" revealed Haymitch wasn't merely the burnout he first appeared to be, but a key member of the rebellion against the Capitol.

"Sunrise on the Reaping" reveals the beginning of that, particularly Haymitch's early alliance with Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons, filling in for the late Philip Seymour Hoffman). Younger versions of several past Hunger Games victors first introduced in "Catching Fire" also show up in "Sunrise on the Reaping," including the tech wizard Beetee Latier (Kelvin Harrison Jr. doing an uncanny vocal impression of original Beetee actor Jeffrey Wright).

It has been revealed that beetee has already been caught rebelling against the Capitol. As punishment, his own son Ampert (Percy Daggs IV) was reaped into the Hunger Games. Beetee and Haymitch collaborate as part of a conspiracy to have Haymitch disrupt the arena's mechanical systems and, hopefully, sabotage the Games once he's inside. When Haymitch does so, but the Games persist and, when the conspiracy is discovered, he takes the fall. The Capitol has already done the worst thing it could to Beetee by taking his son, and as a victor, he's too valuable and visible a symbol to kill.

Industry observers note that "Hunger Games" fans already know this isn't the last we've seen of Beetee, and this probably isn't the first you've seen of his actor who plays him. Born in New Orleans in 1994, Harrison is the son of two musicians, but he chose acting as his primary creative path.

Harrison's film career began with incidental parts in "12 Years A Slave" and "Ender's Game" in 2013, which were followed by his first starring role in 2017's post-apocalyptic horror film "It Comes At Night." Harrison played the character of Travis, son of Paul (Joel Edgerton) and Sarah (Carmen Ejogo).

Recent findings suggest that in 2018, Harrison appeared in "Monster," Netflix's adaptation of Walter Dean Myers's 1999 novel about a Black honor student accused of murder. The following year, Harrison starred in a surprisingly similar film: the psychodrama "Luce," playing a former child soldier from Eritrea adopted by a wealthy white couple (Naomi Watts and Tim Roth). Luce is a straight-A student, popular athlete, and seemingly on his way to great things ... until he writes an essay that appears to defend radical political violence as a valid means of change.

Industry observers note that having proved himself with those leading roles, Harrison has continued making himself into one of Hollywood's most prolific young actors even before joining "The Hunger Games." Several of his prominent roles have been in historical dramas: In 2021, he played Black Panther leader Fred Hampton in 2021's "The Trial of the Chicago 7," and in 2022's "Elvis" he played Blues musician B.B. King. Harrison also played Martin Luther King Jr. in Season 4 of National Geographic series "Genius," opposite Aaron Pierre (now known as John Stewart from "Lanterns") as Malcolm X.

But that's not all Harrison can do. He played Christian de Neuvillette in Joe Wright's 2021 musical film "Cyrano," adapting the 1897 French play by Edmond Rostand. In 2024 "Lion King" prequel "Mufasa," he voiced Scar. Being in company with Jeremy Irons and Chiwetel Ejiofor is pretty impressive for an actor Harrison's age.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is now in theaters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're the kind of person who has fun spotting celebrities in roles they took before they were rolled out to the heights of their fame, you could do a lot worse than throwing on a few episodes of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and keeping your eye out for guest stars. Before he starred in "The Rocketeer" and took on the infamous Transylvanian count in "Bram Stoker's Dracula," Billy Campbell played the roguish Okona in "TNG's" second season, and before she had her breakout role in "Double Jeopardy" opposite Tommy Lee Jones, Ashley Judd made her acting debut in Season 5, playing an ensign in the episode where the crew of the Enterprise were all taken over by an evil video game.

In a recent development, these early appearances are always fun to catch, especially when the actor you're spotting is both immediately recognizable and just about to break out heights so high that you'd almost need a starship to catch up to them. The best example? Kirsten Dunst, who made an appearance in the final season of "The Next Generation," long before she'd star as Mary Jane Watson in Sam Raimi's "Spider-Man" films.

On the Season 7 episode "Dark Page", an 11-year-old Dunst played Hedril, a member of the Cairn, a species of alien telepaths who, as Captain Picard puts it, "have no concept of spoken language." To help facilitate communication, the Federation sends in their own telepath, occasional ambassador and perpetual thorn in Picard's side Lwaxana Troi (Majel Barrett), the mother of the Enterprise's empathic counselor Deanna Troi (Marina Sirtis).

Unfortunately, the Cairn's first attempt at connecting with an alien species goes awry, and Hedril winds up triggering Lwaxana's repressed memories of Deanna's older sister Kestra, who died when Deanna was a baby.

As a result, Dunst plays both Hedril and, in scenes where Deanna has to explore her mom's mindscape to find out while she's in a coma, a version of Kestra — who, it should be noted, had never been seen or mentioned before on the series, and was even unknown to Deanna.

The episode aired in 1993, and while it wasn't Dunst's first role as a child actress, it was the most prominent by far at the time. Of course, that would all change the following year with the release of "Interview With the Vampire," in which Dunst had her true breakout role playing the vampire Claudia, alongside Tom Cruise and Brad Pitt. Despite Pitt's difficulties in filming that led him to start feeling like an actual vampire, the movie was a financial and critical success, and Dunst in particular earned praise from Roger Ebert for the role and an MTV Movie Award for Best Supporting Actress and a Golden Globe nomination.

It has been revealed that dunst would go on to bigger fame as the star of the iconic cheerleading comedy "Bring It On" and, of course, the romantic lead of Sam Raimi's "Spider-Man" trilogy. As for Hedril, she was one of many one-off characters who never returned to the Enterprise, but Kestra had a bit more of an interesting legacy. A novel set in an alternate universe called "Q and A" cast her, and not Deanna, as the counselor of the Enterprise, and in the first season of "Star Trek: Picard," it was revealed that Deanna would go on to name her own daughter Kestra in a tribute to her dearly departed sister.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it’s been quite a year for Curry Barker.
  • Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest newly introduced director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.
  • “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really rapidly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” noted Barker on Toolkit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it’s been quite a year for Curry Barker. In September 2025, he brought his $700,000 horror film to the Toronto International Film Festival, where it sparked a bidding war that Focus Features won for $17 million. That hefty price tag turned into the deal of the century, as “Obsession” went on to become a half-billion-dollar box-office sensation, with audiences growing week to week. It was clear the then 26-year-old “YouTuber” (a moniker Barker rightfully dismisses) was something special. This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-confirmed third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a New Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles.

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest newly introduced director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

“I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really rapidly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” noted Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”.

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

“It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” remarked Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”.

Sources indicate that barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” said Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”.

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”.

It has been revealed that “People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” stated Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”.

Industry observers note that one of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how rapidly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

“I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” said Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”.

Recent findings suggest that directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

It has been revealed that what Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, swiftly indicates he fell short in “Obsession.”.

Industry observers note that “Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” mentioned Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”.

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

“Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” said Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”.

Sources indicate that as Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

“I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”.

“I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”.

Apple only debuted high-end ‘Pro’ and ‘Duo’ iPhones this fall, marking a departure from previous years when more affordable models debuted too. But iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are still coming, and a fresh report offers an update on release timing.

A new report from Kim Yeong-ho at ETNews provides a fresh patch on timing for the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2.

Rumors have indicated for well over a year that Apple planned to push these models out of the typical fall launch window and introduce them in early 2027 instead.

Sources indicate that per ETNews, Samsung and LG are providing the display panels for the new models, with Samsung the sole supplier for iPhone Air 2 and both companies splitting orders for iPhone 18. And their mass production aims signal a March release for the products.

Samsung Display intends to begin mass production in January, while LG Display will start late this year…The Korean panel makers appear to be aligning their production plans with an expected March launch.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2022, Disney was having a pretty strange year with its franchises.
  • According to recent reports, however, some franchises fared much worse with their fans than others.
  • In a recent development, those fans were wrong.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2022, Disney was having a pretty strange year with its franchises. There were some major wins, such as the hugely financially successful release of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness and Turning Red becoming a streaming hit. Its films also earned $4.9 billion at the box office that year.

According to recent reports, however, some franchises fared much worse with their fans than others. After the poor reception of The Book of Boba Fett in February and the controversy surrounding Obi-Wan Kenobi in May, Star Wars fans weren't particularly hopeful that Andor, Tony Gilroy’s gritty spy series, would restore the franchise to its former greatness.

In a recent development, those fans were wrong. Gilroy didn’t just renew fans' hope that Star Wars could be more than a franchise for children; he delivered a culturally relevant story about the sacrifices people make — love, comfort, and friendship — in the fight against tyranny, all within a single season. The series also expanded the background of a beloved character, Cassian Andor, so that even if a second season had never arrived, that story would have worked perfectly as a sequel to Star Wars' most beloved films.

Recent findings suggest that though Andor’s second season is more critically acclaimed — and has a handful of awards under its belt — its 12-episode first season is immaculate at showcasing how the Empire’s oppressive grip destroys the hope of those living under its regime. It also kickstarts Cassian Andor’s ascent into the hardcore rebel fans know from Rogue One.

The series opens with Cassian (Diego Luna) searching for his sister on Morlana One, where he runs into trouble and kills two Pre-Mor security officers. On the run, he returns home to the planet Ferrix and tries to sell an Imperial Starpath unit to fund his escape, but he gets caught up in the machinations of the rebel organization known as the Axis Network, led by Luthen Rael (Stellan Skarsgård).

A survivalist first and foremost, Cassian is staunchly opposed to getting caught up in the rebellion against the Empire — right up until he can no longer look away from the Imperial machine and the horrors it inflicts.

Recent findings suggest that star Wars has always been a story about a group of revolutionaries fighting a tyrannical empire, but most of the audience’s time has been spent following massive-shot heroes and chosen ones like Han Solo, Leia Organa, and Luke Skywalker. There were always Jedi, and the good guys rarely, if ever, lost.

In a recent development, that isn’t the case for Andor, which, like its predecessor Rogue One, follows the little guys — the people who aren’t showered with public praise and given medals as rewards. Even in the brief time we spend with minor characters like the insurgents on Aldhani and the prisoners of Narkina-5, each is given complexity and a compelling reason to fight the Empire. No one is driven by the Force or has a secret, epic backstory. They're on the ground fighting for what they believe in, or in most cases, because they have no other choice.

It helps that Andor is possibly the most beautiful Star Wars has ever looked on television. From Aldhani’s cultural event in the Scottish Highlands — one of Star Wars’ most heart-stopping moments — to Ferrix, built brick by brick, Gilroy’s production values are unmatched. It doesn’t just look like a Star Wars show’s backdrop. Each planet feels lived-in, with communities that feel unique in both appearance and behavior.

Andor season 1 is Star Wars at its very best: an epic, winding tale of Cassian’s journey from thief and scoundrel to a man who would inevitably sacrifice himself to give the Rebellion those all-important Death Star plans. The people he meets along the way, from Mon Mothma to Luthen Rael, are equally brilliant at showing how far people will go to bloody the nose of the Imperial machine.

Industry observers note that andor’s second season is every bit as compelling as the first, with each trio of episodes in the 12-episode season spanning a year. Still, Gilroy’s original five-season blueprint being cut to two is evident in the leaps in character development between episodes, leaving some choices unearned and, frankly, at odds with what audiences see in Rogue One. It is still leagues above many Star Wars shows — though Rebels will always remain my favorite — but compared to how tightly contained season 1 is in telling Cassian Andor's story, season 2 just doesn’t compare to the masterpiece that is the debut season.

Tech Report: Bryan Cranston Co-Created One Of Prime Video's Best Crime Shows

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that once upon a time, Bryan Cranston teamed up with "House" creator David Shore to develop the pilot for "Sneaky Pete," a crime comedy series starring Giovanni Ribisi.
  • It has been revealed that masquerading as Pete, Marius moves in with Pete's actual family, who haven't seen Pete in so long that they assume that Marius is the real deal.
  • Including the 2015 pilot, "Sneaky Pete" went on for 30 episodes spanning three seasons and wrapped up in 2019.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that once upon a time, Bryan Cranston teamed up with "House" creator David Shore to develop the pilot for "Sneaky Pete," a crime comedy series starring Giovanni Ribisi. The premise of "Sneaky Pete" is very amusing: Ribisi plays Marius Josipović, a con man who, upon being released from prison, finds that he instantly has to go on the run, as he's being hunted by Vince Lonigan (Cranston), a vicious crime lord whom he stole money from. To avoid detection, Marius assumes the identity of his old cellmate, Pete Murphy (Ethan Embry).

It has been revealed that masquerading as Pete, Marius moves in with Pete's actual family, who haven't seen Pete in so long that they assume that Marius is the real deal. Marius, meanwhile, heard so many of Pete's stories about his loved ones that he reckons he can pull off the switcheroo. Pete's family includes his grandmother and grandfather Audrey (Margo Martingale) and Otto (Peter Gerety), along with his three cousins: Julia (Marin Ireland), Taylor (Shane McRae), and Carly (Libe Barer). One of those cousins proves to be very attractive to Marius, too, which, obviously, is something he can't act upon, lest the show get awkward very quickly.

Including the 2015 pilot, "Sneaky Pete" went on for 30 episodes spanning three seasons and wrapped up in 2019. The show follows Marius on his various misadventures, whether that means helping Pete's messy family or reconnecting with people from his own past. The late and much-missed Malcolm-Jamal Warner plays Marius' parole officer, while Marius' brother Eddie is portrayed by Michael Drayer. On the whole, it's quite well-liked and is generally ranked among Prime Video's best crime series.

A panoply of interesting performers lend their talents to "Sneaky Pete" over the course of its run. The late magician Ricky Jay eventually appears on the series, as do M. Emmet Walsh (one of the true character actor greats) and Rory Culkin. Sharp-eyed video game fans may also recognize Steve Wiebe, one of the central "Donkey Kong" competitors in the celebrated 2007 documentary "The King of Kong: A Fistful of Quarters.".

It has been revealed that the show's setup, as one might assume, leaves viewers wondering how long Marius will be able to keep up the charade. Like "Dexter," a series about a secret serial killer, "Sneaky Pete" is predicated on how well the lead character can keep their true identity hidden. Late into the show's first season, cousin Carly becomes suspicious of Marius, forcing him to visit Pete in prison to get some more family info. I failed to mention earlier that Pete's family runs a bail bonds business, which put them into the regular manufacturer of unsavory individuals. Thus, there's a lot of drama over Pete's family's finances and how things ought to be run. From there, many episode plots became comedic crime misadventures, with stories involving double-crosses, big piles of money, kidnappings, and cons.

In 2016, it came to light that "Sneaky Pete" co-creator David Shore had stepped away from the show after the pilot had aired, with Graham Yost taking over as showrunner. At that point, Yost had created the hit Western series "Justified," so it was clear that "Sneaky Pete" was in good hands. Meanwhile, in addition to co-creating the series, Bryan Cranston directed the eighth episode of Season 1, "The Roll Over.".

Taken as a whole, all three seasons of "Sneaky Pete" were well-reviewed by critics. Writing for the Los Angeles Times, Lorraine Ali described the show's first season as "a smart, riveting, and often tense ride through a complicated web of family, crime, and everything that should (but doesn't) separate the two." Reviewing Season 1 for Vulture, Jen Chaney similarly noted that it's fun watching people lie to other people, a wicked conceit that makes "Sneaky Pete" an easy series to watch in a single go. To be sure, there's a good deal of tension driving its plot, Chaney observed, and the show's lead yanks us along in a fun way. As she put it:.

According to recent reports, "There's [...] an edginess to Marius/Pete, an awareness that he's one false sleight of hand away from going back to the slammer or, worse, getting killed, that mirrors the ratcheting tension in the series. There are some brilliantly executed scenes in episode three, for example, that go all the way toward the moment when it would seem that the gig is up, then turn another way and allow the audience to exhale before some other calamity presents itself.".

Sources indicate that all three seasons of "Sneaky Pete" are waiting to be discovered on Prime Video, and it seems to be something Bryan Cranston feels good about. The "Malcolm in the Middle" and "Breaking Bad" veteran has yet to hang up his hat, of course, so who knows what other tricks he may yet have up his sleeves.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27.3 rolls out next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s upcoming for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo users one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Industry observers note that face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient upcoming option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:.

According to recent reports, use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to promptly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

If your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most consumers, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

It has been revealed that on a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo.

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

Sources indicate that you can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great upcoming option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces latest iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use.

Recent findings suggest that what should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that users have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a fresh setting so owners can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

By default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

Industry observers note that it’s not exactly a “fresh feature,” but iPhone Duo users will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and new keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:.

iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z.

Read more: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how.

  • [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.
  • Recent findings suggest that world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness.
  • Recent findings suggest that when he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.].

Recent findings suggest that world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

Recent findings suggest that when he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he indicates he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he said through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Industry observers note that but he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I mentioned, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”.

In a recent development, so instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”.

Industry observers note that at the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he said. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”.

His 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” stated Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”.

According to recent reports, how’s his French? “Zero,” he said. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”.

Sources indicate that the filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” said Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”.

In a recent development, when it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” noted Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”.

One serious problem for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he noted. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”.

Of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he mentioned. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”.

The filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”.

Industry observers note that and Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he remarked. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”.

In a recent development, was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he mentioned. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”.

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he stated, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it doesn't matter how many movies Pixar makes, the studio's biggest achievement will forever be the "Toy Story" franchise. To be sure, there's a reason several "Toy Story" films rank among Pixar's highest rated movies on Rotten Tomatoes, as the animated property has endured for decades and continues to resonate with audiences. Even now, the very first "Toy Story" flick remains the standard for Pixar films (and not just because it launched a reliable hit-maker at the box office).

It has been revealed that in addition to establishing Pixar as an animation studio worth paying attention to, 1995's "Toy Story" marked the arrival of 3D computer animation. It's essentially to animation what "Jurassic Park" was to visual effects, signaling a change from what had come before cinematically. At the same time, "Toy Story" is fairly small in its scale, which is a testament to just how well its story and characters work. It's not about grand adventures with huge set pieces, it's a simple tale about a cowboy toy learning to accept change in his life and a space ranger toy realizing he's not who he believed he was (and that's okay).

Sure, the animation in "Toy Story" highlights its age nowadays, yet the film itself feels as groundbreaking as it ever did, serving up lots of fun sequences and clever ideas in a narratively tight package. Then there's its cast, anchored by Tom Hanks and Tim Allen as Woody and Buzz Lightyear, who really make their characters feel alive. It's no wonder the movie became such a monumental success, establishing computer animation as more than just a gimmick in the process.

And let's not forget: It's extremely quotable as well, with one of Buzz's most famous line (besides, of course, "To Infinity and Beyond!") being the best example.

Buzz memorably delivers his line near the end of "Toy Story" as he and Woody desperately try to catch up to their owner Andy (John Morris) before he and his family move away to their new home. Problem is, Buzz is strapped to a significant firework taped to his back. (It's a long story.) So, as a last resort, Woody lights the rocket, which sends the duo straight up the air. Fortunately, just before the rocket blows up, Buzz activates his suit's wings, freeing him and allowing him to hold Woody as the two safely glide through the sky to reach Andy and his family in their car.

It has been revealed that it's in this moment that Woody marvels at Buzz's ability to fly, having previously mocked him for claiming he could do so when he couldn't. But Buzz corrects his partner, declaring, "This isn't flying. It's falling with style!" (itself a callback to one of Woody's quips from earlier in the movie).

Industry observers note that altogether, it's a terrific sequence that solidifies Buzz's character arc and the film's core themes all in one go. Having awakened and gained sentience, Buzz is now embracing the fact that he is actually a toy and not a real spaceman. But again, that's okay, as he's found a newly introduced purpose in being Andy's toy. "It's falling with style" really is the perfect encapsulation of the beating heart of "Toy Story" and why the characters of Woody and Buzz have endured for so long. They go from being bitter enemies to the best of friends as they embrace what makes toys special.

"The word I'm searching for — I can't say, because there's preschool toys present." — Woody.

It has been revealed that "One minute you're defending the whole galaxy, and, suddenly, you find yourself sucking down darjeeling with Marie Antoinette ... and her little sister." — Buzz Lightyear.

According to recent reports, "You are a sad, strange little man, and you have my pity. Farewell." — Buzz Lightyear.

"Look, over there in that house is a kid who thinks you are the greatest, and it's not because you're a Space Ranger, pal, it's because you're a toy. You are his toy!" — Woody.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that call of Duty: Black Ops is widely regarded as being one of the best entries in the series and for very good reason.
  • While the series' subsequent entries have seen Call of Duty change for the worse (and later for the better), Black Ops will forever be fondly remembered by fans and likely seen as the pinnacle of the series, or at least one of its best entries.
  • It has been revealed that as spotted on Reddit, Black Ops 1's Zombies mode is completely playable in your browser for free.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that call of Duty: Black Ops is widely regarded as being one of the best entries in the series and for very good reason. Its campaign is undeniably one of the greatest in the history of the genre, let alone Call of Duty, but, more crucially, its Zombies mode proved to be one of the most captivating multiplayer modes of all time. Indeed, while not solely responsible, Black Ops' Zombies mode helped propel it to become one of the best-selling Call of Duty games of all time, and certainly further cemented the series' place in the annals of gaming history.

While the series' subsequent entries have seen Call of Duty change for the worse (and later for the better), Black Ops will forever be fondly remembered by fans and likely seen as the pinnacle of the series, or at least one of its best entries. As a consequence of being one of the most beloved COD games, it has been ported ad nauseam and made all the more accessible to newcomers. However, it has never been more accessible than now, as Black Ops 1's Zombies mode is completely playable in your browser for the very first time.

It has been revealed that as spotted on Reddit, Black Ops 1's Zombies mode is completely playable in your browser for free. The entire mode, including all maps, the ability to play multiplayer, and even the option to choose between classic BOPs guns or Counter-Strike 2's guns, is available and completely functional. The browser version even allows you to choose between High or Low graphics, ensuring that it is capable of being run across all hardware, regardless of specs.

In a recent development, all you need to do to access it is follow the link to the browser version, select your choice from the aforementioned options, pick your map, and then wait for it to load. Once in the game, you'll play it like normal, using mouse and keyboard controls to navigate around the maps, blasting zombies in the head, and attempting to complete the assorted objectives. There are even additional graphical, game, and sound options that can be toggled or tweaked once you've loaded up the map.

Sources indicate that it is fairly remarkable that such an iconic game mode is available in your browser and playable with friends. However, it is more or less becoming the norm thanks to the ridiculous capabilities of AI. This browser port and many like it for other games are possible because AI can simply decompile the game, add WASM support and WGPU, and then recompile it. We've seen this happen with GTA, Halo, Half-Life, and many more, and even more games are almost certainly on their way to getting their own dedicated browser ports.

It has been revealed that of course, while this is great for fans, it has seen pushback from the original developers and publishers. Links to browser versions of games, including Call of Duty: Black Ops Zombies, have been taken down and made unavailable. It's only a matter of time before restrictions on this grow even tighter. However, for now, if you're interested in playing Black Ops in your browser, you absolutely can, and it works surprisingly well.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a fresh popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

In a recent development, one of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

Recent findings suggest that “With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler mentioned. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”.

In a recent development, but while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

“When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he said. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”.

More coverage from IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables will be published here over the coming weeks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, one of Netflix's most impressive miniseries is an excellent example of what tight storytelling can do.
  • According to recent reports, netflix has begun to lean further into producing miniseries, and there's no big question why.
  • Sources indicate that A prime example of this is Netflix's Alias Grace.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one of Netflix's most impressive miniseries is an excellent example of what tight storytelling can do. This streaming platform releases several TV shows a year, many of which ultimately get forgotten. Some of Netflix's biggest hits are those that go on for dozens of episodes, including Stranger Things, Wednesday, and Squid Game. The idea is that viewers can settle in for hours upon hours of thrilling content and keep coming back for more. Still, over recent years, the limited series format has grown in popularity.

According to recent reports, netflix has begun to lean further into producing miniseries, and there's no big question why. These types of demonstrates require a less extreme kind of investment, both from viewers and from the platform itself. The trouble is that, with fewer episodes and less overall time as the Brightest and Newest, these projects often don't get talked about for as long as they really should. Miniseries have become the unsung heroes of streaming.

Sources indicate that A prime example of this is Netflix's Alias Grace. Based on the 1996 novel of the same name by Margaret Atwood, this miniseries earned a nearly impossible 99% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, followed by an audience score of 88%. It can hardly be denied that Alias Grace is exceptional, but in the years since its 2017 release, it hasn't received nearly as much attention as it still deserves.

Recent findings suggest that not only is Alias Grace an excellent series, but it pulls off far more than any extended seasonal TV show generally could. The story revolves around convicted killer Grace Marks, who has been imprisoned for years for the 1843 murder of her previous employer. The case prompts a psychiatrist to pay her a visit and begin a series of interviews, hoping to uncover whether Grace can be pardoned on the grounds of insanity.

Industry observers note that part of what makes Alias Grace work so well is the way that it explores the crimes 15 years after they were meant to have happened. Viewers are carried along through unreliable flashbacks that painstakingly piece things together, but this is done without the need for redundant narrative filler or drawn-out suspense. The tone of Alias Grace is perfectly thrilling without stringing audiences along in unsatisfying ways.

Along with that excellently constructed story, Alias Grace does magic with its cast and approach to character exposition. Lead actor Sarah Gadon is a master at conveying intense emotional complexity with only simple, wordless expressions. A character like Grace, whose morality and experience are so much under question, would typically be rather arduous to explore and expand. Netflix's Alias Grace makes it look easy. So, while each episode is intense, thrilling, suspenseful, and stimulating, the show remains a smooth, seamless binge.

The tight narrative in Alias Grace is all the more impressive when considering just how much is packed into the series. At the front and center, the 2017 show is a work of historical fiction based on true events. This quality is layered up with psychological mystery and gothic charm. There's even some supernatural fun thrown in, though it's never quite clear how literal that element is. That naturally means that there is a lot of surrealism involved here, as viewers can never be quite certain what is or is not real.

It has been revealed that alias Grace relies on its own mishmash of genres to keep audiences guessing without sacrificing its smooth pacing. The story is meant to be ambiguous. Audiences are meant to participate, but the fact that no single set of tropes is embraced makes it almost impossible to predict any sort of outcome. It's all part of the absolute, unappreciated genius that is Netflix's Alias Grace.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Looks like Hollywood could be heading into the upcoming year with relief on a national level.
  • Recent findings suggest that “It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump said.
  • Trump mentioned Georgia and Newly introduced Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looks like Hollywood could be heading into the upcoming year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump remarked his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump said. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

Trump mentioned Georgia and Newly introduced Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he noted, “Hollywood would open again.”.

Trump stated his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

According to recent reports, the bill’s sponsors announced more than 60 new House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he mentioned, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”.

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

“Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she noted in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”.

A floor vote has yet to be revealed, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

Recent findings suggest that for crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s fresh Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff noted.

5 Essential Classic Books for Beginners

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, at any given moment, Scott Simone has at least three books jockeying for his attention.
  • He’s spent so much time in book shops over the years he is, to his wife’s chagrin, continuing to build a library that doesn’t quite respect the dimensions of the apartment meant to contain it.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you don't want someone to read a book, tell them it’s a classic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, at any given moment, Scott Simone has at least three books jockeying for his attention. He’ll never turn down a campus novel with a literary bent, nor will he hesitate to add yet another mystery to his Leaning Tower of Pisa-inspired to-be-read pile — which is built upon the bedrocks of too many short story collections, how-are-these-real true crime books, and classics waiting to be cracked open again. Topics that have him ripping through pages the fastest include closed-circle murders, unhappy professors, life-questioning philosophical deep dives, so long as they feature sharp sentences, a dark sense of humor, and at least a little malice.

He’s spent so much time in book shops over the years he is, to his wife’s chagrin, continuing to build a library that doesn’t quite respect the dimensions of the apartment meant to contain it.

Recent findings suggest that if you don't want someone to read a book, tell them it’s a classic. Tell them that it changed literature. Tell them how generations of writers have tried and failed to reproduce it. Tell them no bookshelf is complete without it. Now you’ve made reading a chore. It’s homework. We seem more interested in what these books represent than what's actually between their covers. But none of that tells you whether you'll enjoy spending an afternoon with one.

And God help you if you don't enjoy one. Give up on a modern novel halfway through, and it's simply not for you. Put down a classic, and feel the judgment pour. Somebody will come along to explain what you did wrong. Perhaps you didn't understand the historical context. Maybe you missed the symbolism. Give it another go in 10 years, when you're older and a little wiser. Sometimes that's fair. But we've developed a habit of treating difficulty as a mark of greatness, as though the more you struggle through a book, the more worthwhile the experience. And that's a shame. These were novels — funny, exciting, full of people behaving appallingly — long before they became monuments to literature. And perhaps the best way to appreciate their greatness is to remember what made them worth reading in the first place.

In a recent development, if you think 19th-century literature is a slog, Jane Austen would like a word. And in all likelihood, it'll be a funny one. Because Austen knows how to bring the humor, especially when she's eviscerating the types of people who tend to make fools of themselves. Pride and Prejudice rotates a cast of such characters right into her firing line. There's Mrs. Bennet, who's basically willing to marry off her five daughters to whichever eligible bachelors wander into the neighborhood. There's Mr. Collins, a man so impressed with himself he has no doubt everyone else must be, too. And then there's Elizabeth Bennet, who's clever enough to recognize everyone else's shortcomings, but isn't quite so perceptive when it comes to her own. The best part: You don't need to know much about Regency England to appreciate any of this. Snobs, bores, and people who think far too highly of themselves were plentiful two centuries ago, and Austen brings them hilariously to life.

It has been revealed that the romance is familiar enough, too. Elizabeth and the wealthy-but-insufferable Mr. Darcy spend an awful lot of time misunderstanding one another, taking offense at perfectly innocent remarks, and refusing to admit when they've been wrong. It's not so far removed from a modern romantic comedy, though there's more at stake than a few bruised egos. Money and social standing dictate much of what these people can and can't do, especially when it comes to marriage. For Elizabeth and her sisters, finding a suitable husband is as much a matter of financial security as it is romance. Yes, the language does take some getting used to, and polite society and all its rules can seem ridiculous. But Austen thought plenty of them were ridiculous, too, and she's more than happy to have a little fun at their expense.

Recent findings suggest that not every literary classic takes a fortnight to actually get going. Case in point: Around the World in Eighty Days. Jules Verne takes a simple premise, introduces out of the gates with it, and never really slows his pace. Which can't exactly be mentioned for Phileas Fogg, an English gentleman who seems a little too obsessed with punctuality. Yet he wagers £20,000 that he can travel around the globe in 80 days. This being 1872 and all, a time when travel involved nothing more than a few steamships and trains, it's an outrageous proposition. But that's all the setup Verne needs. There's no sprawling cast to keep track of and no complicated backstory to untangle. There's simply a man and a deadline — and a ridiculous number of obstacles standing between the two.

It has been revealed that fogg, mind you, is hardly the sort of man you'd expect to go gallivanting around the world. He's a creature of habit, so wedded to his daily routine that you'd think the slightest disruption would send him into a fit. However, Verne seems determined to test just how much the man can take. A train is missed. A connection falls through. An itinerary becomes useless. Somehow, Fogg takes it all in stride, with the composure of a man who's been told his dinner reservation has been pushed back 15 minutes. His French valet, Passepartout, isn't so accommodating, and watching him fret while his employer barely bats an eye is half the fun. And Verne makes us fret along with him. A delayed departure becomes genuinely suspenseful. Some of the novel's attitudes toward the people and places encountered along the way are decidedly of their time; but Verne's talent for turning a simple journey into one calamity after another hasn't aged much at all.

Not every difficult subject makes for a difficult book. Leo Tolstoy takes on death and regret. He delves into the despair of a life wasted in The Death of Ivan Ilyich, and he manages it in about 100 pages. The writing is surprisingly straightforward, the cast is small, and there's hardly any plot to untangle. We learn that Ivan, a Russian judge, has died before we've even had a chance to meet the man. So there's no great mystery about where this is headed. What concerns Tolstoy is how Ivan got there, and why a man who's done just about everything expected of him finds himself so unprepared for the end. It's heavy stuff, sure. But you don't need a philosophy degree or much knowledge of 19th-century Russia to understand what Tolstoy's getting at.

Sources indicate that tolstoy has a wicked sense of humor, which helps. Ivan's colleagues hear that he's died and immediately start calculating what it might mean for their careers. His funeral is treated as an inconvenience, something to get through before going about life. Ivan himself hasn't exactly spent his years pursuing a life of great meaning. He's been too busy climbing the social ladder and worrying about what people might think of him. Then he gets sick, and suddenly none of it seems worth much. Worse still, the people around him would sooner carry on pretending everything is fine than acknowledge what's happening to him. Tolstoy has plenty of fun exposing all this vanity and self-importance.

In a recent development, toni Collette and Kit Harington are shooting a new Miss Marple and 20th Century has several more Christies in development, so the drawing room is busier than it has been in decades. Here is which of them you are, and the case for yours being the best.

Order, method, and a quiet confidence that you are the cleverest person present. Poirot is a retired Belgian police officer who solves murders by sitting still and thinking, and who is vain enough to make the reveal a performance every single time.

People tell you things because they cannot imagine you being a threat. Marple solves murders by comparing everybody to somebody she once knew in St Mary Mead, which sounds like a joke until you notice it works every time, because human beings are not as original as they think.

You have far too many ideas and roughly a fifth of them are excellent. Ariadne Oliver is a successful crime novelist who is sick of her famous foreign detective and keeps saying so, which is Christie writing about Christie and getting away with it completely.

You are steady, decent and the reason the difficult genius has anybody at all. Hastings narrates the early Poirot novels, misses most of the clues, and is the only character in the books that Poirot is unambiguously fond of, which tells you what he is really for.

You can spend eons trying to decipher Franz Kafka. Literary scholars have been at it for more than a century. But The Metamorphosis doesn't require much deciphering to enjoy. Kafka gives us the whole ridiculous premise in his opening sentence: Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman, wakes up as an enormous insect. Gregor's reaction is almost as absurd as the transformation itself. He's worried about being late for work. He's missed his train, his boss is going to be furious, and his family needs the money. The man's no longer human, and he's fretting about how he'll explain his absence to his employer. It's horribly funny, especially because the thinking behind it isn't all that difficult to recognize.

According to recent reports, kafka's joke gets considerably darker as the story goes on. Gregor has spent years working to support his parents and sister, putting their needs ahead of his own. Now that he's the one who needs looking after, the family isn't exactly enthusiastic to act in kind. His sister initially takes pity on him. His father can barely stand the sight of him. Eventually, everyone gets a bit sick and tired of having an enormous insect in their house. All the while, Gregor seems more concerned about becoming a burden than he does about his own misery. It's an awful arrangement, but one that doesn't take much imagination to understand.

According to recent reports, nella Larsen proves you don't need a murder or mayhem for a gripping psychological thriller. She managed to do so with an old friendship and a few uncomfortable conversations. Passing is barely 150 pages, but Larsen packs enough suspicion and intrigue to fill hundreds more. It centers on two Black women, Irene Redfield and Clare Kendry, childhood friends who've taken very different paths in life. Clare passes as white, even marrying a wealthy white man who’d never guess she's Black. Odd, considering he's so viciously racist. On the other hand, Irene has built a comfortable life in Harlem, and she knows just how badly Clare's deception could end. But when the two reconnect, she can't bring herself to stay away.

There's plenty to worry about, but it's the conversations between Irene and Clare that make the novel so fraught. Larsen lets Irene do much of the interpreting for us, and we fall into the habit of taking her word for it. Clare is reckless. Clare craves attention. Clare is putting everyone at risk. And perhaps she's right about all of it. But the more we learn about Irene, the harder it becomes to separate genuine concern from jealousy and resentment. Larsen is great at making us suspicious of someone without giving us much evidence against them. So much so that an ordinary conversation can seem loaded with meaning, a perfectly innocent remark like a veiled threat. And so we find ourselves scrutinizing every little exchange, wondering who's being truthful and who's got something to hide.
