#97048. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2890 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer claims it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to substantial issues.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • In a recent development, andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer claims it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to substantial issues.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

In a recent development, andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his organization Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to major concerns in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

It has been revealed that andrew Ng: This is a substantial question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having noted that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having mentioned that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of owners, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing manufacturer with millions of consumers.

In a recent development, ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from massive data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

Industry observers note that I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

In a recent development, over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing latest here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and stated, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

Industry observers note that the data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one tech giant or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that indicated up.

According to recent reports, you often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Recent findings suggest that ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from significant data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

Industry observers note that when you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having stated that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an notable piece of the puzzle.

It has been revealed that one of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is notable, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an vital tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

According to recent reports, ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

Industry observers note that “In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

Industry observers note that synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

Sources indicate that to make these problems more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a firm approaches Landing AI and states it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

According to recent reports, ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

Sources indicate that one of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Industry observers note that ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really key to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

Recent findings suggest that in the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion owners. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

In a recent development, ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent newly introduced neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s crucial for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print concern as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

5 Thriller Movies We Actually Want To See a Remake Of

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1405 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that feel free to connect with him or check out his work.
  • It has been revealed that remakes have a bad reputation, and unfortunately, most of the time, they have earned it.
  • Sources indicate that A straight copy of a classic thriller has almost no suspense left to offer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

It has been revealed that remakes have a bad reputation, and unfortunately, most of the time, they have earned it. The problem is that studios love banking on famous titles and hoping nostalgia will do the heavy lifting. That doesn’t really work with the thriller genre, where the whole experience depends on not knowing what happens next. Once audiences know the twist, there is very little reason to sit through the same story again.

Sources indicate that A straight copy of a classic thriller has almost no suspense left to offer. This means that the thrillers that are actually worth remaking are a little different. They’re the ones with brilliant setups that were either held back by their era or were way ahead of their time, with their fears feeling more real today than ever before. Here is a list of five thriller movies people actually want to see remade, as long as they have the right filmmakers behind them.

Recent findings suggest that dead Calm is a thriller that only needs three people and a lot of open water. The film follows Nicole Kidman and Sam Neill as Rae and John Ingram, a married couple who set out on a long sailing trip across the Pacific to grieve after their young son is killed in a car accident. Out in the middle of nowhere, they spot a man named Hughie (Billy Zane) frantically rowing away from a sinking ship. Hughie claims that the rest of his crew died of food poisoning, but when John rows over to investigate, the bodies he discovers tell a very different story. By then, Hughie has taken off in the couple’s yacht, and Rae is trapped aboard with him.

In a recent development, the best thing about Dead Calm is how simple it is. The film is a cat-and-mouse game with nowhere to run and nobody coming to help. What’s even better is that director Phillip Noyce squeezes every bit of tension out of this narrative. That complexity makes it a natural fit for a modern remake. A new version would just need to deal with the fact that satellite phones and GPS make getting stranded at sea much harder today, which could actually add an interesting twist to the story. All a Dead Calm remake needs is a smart director and two strong leads to become the kind of adrenaline-fueled, nerve-wracking thriller that has been missing from the major screen for a while now.

Brian De Palma’s Blow Out bombed at the box office when it first came out, but it has since been recognized as one of the greatest conspiracy thrillers ever made. The film stars John Travolta as sound-effects technician Jack Terry, who works on cheap slasher movies. One night, while recording sounds in a park, Jack captures a car swerving off a bridge and into the river. He manages to rescue a young woman named Sally (Nancy Allen) from the wreck, but the man driving, a governor who was planning to run for president, is killed. When Jack plays back his tape, he hears something that sounds like a gunshot right before the tire blows out, and he soon realizes he has recorded a murder that powerful people want covered up.

In a recent development, blow Out is a thriller story about how easily the truth can be buried, and that idea feels even more relevant now. In 1981, Jack’s audio tape was the only proof that something was wrong. A modern remake of the film could explore what happens when evidence can be faked, edited, or dismissed as a deepfake in seconds. Jack’s obsession with proving what he heard would hit even harder in a world where nobody knows what to believe anymore. The original’s devastating ending is also a significant part of why audiences rejected it back then, but it works perfectly today. Blow Out is a near-perfect film, but its central idea is begging to be updated for the age of misinformation.

In a recent development, marathon Man is the movie that made an entire generation afraid of going to the dentist. The story follows history graduate Babe Levy (Dustin Hoffman), who spends his free time training for a marathon. His life is turned upside down when his older brother, Doc (Roy Scheider), turns out to be a secret government agent who has gotten tangled up with Dr. Christian Szell (Laurence Olivier), a Nazi war criminal hiding in South America. What’s worse is that Szell has come to Newly introduced York to collect a fortune in stolen diamonds, and he is convinced that Babe knows something that could put them at risk. Marathon Man, written by William Goldman from his own novel, is famous for the scene where Szell tortures Babe with dental tools, along with the one where Holocaust survivors recognize him on the streets of New York’s diamond district.

Olivier’s menacing performance earned him an Oscar nomination for the role and practically defined the film. Hoffman also deserves his flowers for portraying Babe’s confusion with extreme conviction, which made the audience sympathize with him every step of the way. Nearly 50 years later, the idea of a war criminal hiding in plain sight, protected by money and powerful friends, still feels frighteningly relevant. Most younger viewers have never seen the original, though, and a fresh version could introduce them to one of the most unsettling stories the genre has ever produced.

Sources indicate that the Parallax View is the ultimate paranoid thriller, and it might be even more unsettling today than it was in the 1970s. The film begins with the assassination of a U.S. senator at the top of Seattle’s Space Needle. Years later, reporter Joe Frady (Warren Beatty) notices that witnesses to the killing keep dying one after another. His investigation leads him to the Parallax Corporation, a shadowy manufacturer that seems to be recruiting troubled men and training them to become assassins.

The film, directed by Alan J. Pakula, who also made All the President’s Men, was released at a time when Americans had lost faith in the people in charge after a string of political assassinations and the Watergate scandal. Its most famous scene is a disturbing montage that Parallax uses to test its recruits, where people are shown flashing images of family and patriotism alongside violence until it’s hard to tell the difference. That idea of a tech giant quietly searching for angry, lonely men to manipulate feels eerily close to how online radicalization works today. A remake could easily swap the old-fashioned test for social media algorithms, and it would be just as terrifying. Paramount+ announced aims for a series version back in 2021, but there has been little news since, and The Parallax View is long overdue for an update.

Wait Until Dark features one of the scariest showdowns in movie history, and it’s the perfect candidate for a remake. The film, based on Frederick Knott’s play, stars Audrey Hepburn as Susy Hendrix, a woman who recently lost her sight and lives in a New York City apartment with her husband, Sam (Efrem Zimbalist Jr.). Without realizing it, Sam brings home a doll that has been stuffed with heroin, and a group of criminals led by the ruthless Roat (Alan Arkin) will do anything to get it back. They come up with an elaborate con to trick Susy into handing it over, but it turns out she is not one to underestimate.

Recent findings suggest that the film’s climax is what most people remember it for. Susy realizes that if she can’t see, the best way to win is to make sure nobody else can either, and she smashes every light in the apartment. When the film first came out, some theaters even dimmed their lights to make the sequence feel even scarier. The problem is that much of the first half has aged poorly, since almost everyone around Susy treats her like a helpless child. A remake could keep the brilliant premise while giving Susy the strength and intelligence she deserves from the very first scene. Hepburn earned an Oscar nomination for the role, but Wait Until Dark is ready for a brand-new heroine who can outsmart her attackers right from the start.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that alien: Isolation 2 has massive moon boots to fill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that alien: Isolation 2 is a rare treat that would’ve been difficult to predict. Indeed, the fact that Alien: Isolation is receiving a sequel more than a decade later is a testament to how profoundly influential it’s been for the horror genre. There’s no doubt that the Alien/Aliens franchise is well-established in horror, but Alien: Isolation is arguably the one Alien video game to most faithfully and authentically represent that horror.

In a recent development, alien: Isolation 2 had a playable demo featured at Gamescom in August, and it may not be much longer before the game is fully released. Regardless, thanks to how many heavy hitters it could boast, 2027 is swiftly taking shape as one of the best years for horror games in a while.

Industry observers note that alien: Isolation 2 has massive moon boots to fill. It’ll be neat to see whether stealth has been significantly improved, for instance, and whether the sequel is as long as its predecessor (one of the biggest critiques of Alien: Isolation to this day being that it’s exceedingly long).

It has been revealed that as to whether or not Alien: Isolation 2 will have a physical edition, Creative Assembly’s response in a Dev Q&A video was incredibly encouraging: “Staying true to the analogue nature of Alien is one of our core pillars. Alien: Isolation 2 will have a physical edition.” This guarantees that the studio is at least eyeing a 2027 release window, considering that PlayStation’s shift toward an all-digital future goes into full effect in early 2028, though it’s possible that it’ll only have physical editions for the consoles that accommodate it by the time it actually launches.

Assuming that Alien: Isolation 2 isn’t delayed, this highly anticipated sequel could be horror’s crown jewel in 2027. 12 years after the launch of the first game, 2027 will be a celebration of the stealth-oriented, first-person-perspective horror games that Alien: Isolation and its ilk directly inspired, as well as other unique horror games in general.

Recent findings suggest that launching in 2027 are The Lost Wild, a dinosaur survival horror game whose game director was Alien: Isolation’s lead designer, and Ontos, a psychological horror game from Amnesia: The Dark Descent and Soma’s Frictional Games. Both are horror. Plus, there are plenty of indie horror games that may not already be on your radar, such as the low-poly Resident Evil and Dark Souls-esque game False Oath.

Of course, Resident Evil Veronica being slated for 2027 ensures that the year will be thrilling nonetheless. Resident Evil Veronica ironically has the lightest weight on its shoulders of any Resident Evil remake to come before it (let alone any remake that follows it). That said, Resident Evil Veronica is much more of a black sheep and may not have as many fans in its corner as the Resident Evil 4 remake or Resident Evil Requiem did, perhaps because Resident Evil Code: Veronica is likely the mainline entry that the fewest fans have played.

Sources indicate that beginning with the launch of the Silent Hill 2 remake, Silent Hill has given itself the unenviable task of releasing a new game every year—Silent Hill 2’s remake in 2024, Silent Hill f in 2025, and Silent Hill: Townfall in 2026. There hasn’t been any confirmation regarding whether or not Bloober’s Silent Hill 1 remake will launch in 2027, but it would certainly align with the franchise’s newfound annual release schedule.

Industry observers note that it’d be sad if Silent Hill misses out on such a fantastic year for horror, especially when the series’ installments have been fairly great lately. Moreover, fans can look forward to ILL and Until Dawn 2, with Until Dawn 2 being particularly exciting for anyone who adored the original Until Dawn and feels as though Supermassive’s choice-driven games still haven’t exceeded its golden standard. Either way, 2027 will be dominated by the horror genre, and Alien: Isolation 2 would be the icing on its cake.

After moving back to upstate Upcoming York last year, I've discovered that the secret to surviving winter is to get outside. Trail running, hiking, snowshoeing — I even tried skiing for the first time, and now that I know I enjoy it enough to justify the cost of the (very expensive) hobby, I'm taking advantage of early Black Friday deals to stock up on the snow-friendly staples missing from my wardrobe.

Luckily, REI's Holiday Sale is happening at just the right time. Now through November 23, you can save up to 61% off on top outdoor brands, including Patagonia, HOKA, and Halfdays. Here are the 11 deals I'm shopping, including base layers, hiking boots, and cold-weather running apparel.

A lighter ski shell jacket is one of the bigger-ticket purchases of the sport. The Patagonia Upstride Jacket is stretchy, water-repellent, and breathable. I especially like that it has plenty of pockets for stashing the little essentials (read: phone and chapstick) you'll want within reach on the mountain.

A good pair of goggles is next on my list, and this Dakine pair comes with two interchangeable lenses, including one designed for low-light conditions. The magnetic lens-swap system is a particularly nice feature, making it easy to adjust when the clouds inevitably roll in.

In a recent development, with the Hoka Transport Hike GTX boots, a little snow and slush won't keep you off the trails. These boots boast a waterproof GORE-TEX membrane to keep feet dry, and the supportive, cushioned design makes them a practical pick for everything from quick walks to longer hikes.

I recently scored the Halfdays Lawrence jacket in Spritz, so now I’m on the lookout for base layers in the same flashy color. These leggings have a high-rise fit and a just right amount of compression, plus the moisture-wicking fabric will keep me comfortable as I work up a sweat (bonus: there's mesh ventilation around the calves where my boots will trap extra heat). And while they're technically designed to work under ski pants, they're cute enough to wear for all sorts of adventures.

This Patagonia base layer is designed to trap warmth while wicking away sweat, and the quarter-zip neckline makes it easy to regulate your temperature. It's the kind of versatile pullover I'd reach for whether I'm heading out for a run or spending the day on the slopes.

Not every winter outing calls for technical gear. This Fjällräven parka features lightweight synthetic insulation, buttoned cuffs, a two-way zipper, and a fixed, adjustable hood. It's ideal for staying warm while running errands thanks to it's slightly longer silhouette, offering more protection against bitter winds.

It has been revealed that merino wool naturally helps regulate temperature while managing moisture. This Smartwool crew is made from 100% merino wool, making it a great foundation for layering under a fleece or jacket. It's also versatile enough to wear on its own when temperatures are a little more forgiving.

Lightweight with an elastic hood, this Vuori jacket will keep you warm on winter runs. The design features a four-way stretch and a water-repellent finish to help protect against mist and snow, while the breathable mesh underarm panels make it a smart option for higher-intensity activities.

Sources indicate that as someone still learning to ski, I love the idea of Arc'teryx bibs. This overall style with adjustable straps will stay securely in place, no matter how many times I take a tumble. The GORE-TEX PRO fabric is waterproof and windproof, while the Dope Permeair™ 20 liner is highly breathable. To say they're an investment would be an understatement, but with their durable construction and thoughtful details, I know I'll be wearing them for many seasons to come.

Sources indicate that I don't plan on giving up my regular running routine just because the temperatures drop. With plush cushioning and grippy traction, these are a particularly good option if your routes take you from paved paths to packed-down trails. Senior writer, Nick Harris-Fry, dubs them “the most versatile running shoe” he’s ever tested in his Hoka Challenger 8 review.

Sources indicate that after the slopes, my hair has a tendency to turn into one giant knot. This chunky, colorblocked beanie by Arc'teryx will hide my bird's nest and keep my ears warm. It's crafted from 100% merino wool, naturally wicking away moisture, regulating temperature, and resisting odors, making it a worthwhile splurge.

For five-plus years, she's covered all things home, from floor covering and furniture to splurge-worthy pillows and budget-friendly bedding. Her work has also appeared on Domino and Saveur.

How Beta Technologies Is Clearing the Runway for Electric Flight

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5433 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network.
  • Beta Technologies, one of the top three U.S.
  • In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network.

Beta Technologies, one of the top three U.S. electric aircraft makers, is aiming first at regional cargo and medical transport, before pursuing the passenger market. Shown here is Beta’s Alia A250, for vertical takeoffs and landings.

In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward.

At the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration.

In a recent development, within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left.

Recent findings suggest that caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right. Despite its 15-meter wingspan, the Alia feels snappy, its fly-by-wire system automatically coordinating aileron and rudder inputs. The machine, he indicates, is much simpler to manage than the Cessna 182 I flew around Australia in my student-pilot days.

What’s more, our half-hour flight in the Alia will consume only about US $9 worth of electricity. The same flight in a comparable Cessna 208 Caravan would burn roughly 25 to 30 gallons of Jet A fuel, costing about $210 to $255 at press time. “Even at full throttle, we’re not burning any fuel up here,” states Caputo, as he takes the Alia into a sweeping left turn and heads south over the lake. “We’re not polluting the environment. [There’s] no noise pollution.”.

At Beta’s South Burlington, Vt., facility, workers assemble the body of an Alia A250. The tech giant says it has an order and option-to-buy backlog of nearly 1,000 aircraft.Beta Technologies.

It has been revealed that this ride is happening during an unusually lively time for electric aviation. The promise of lower operating costs and cleaner flight has pushed electric aircraft from a fringe experiment to one of the aviation industry’s most closely watched frontiers. After years of renderings, prototypes, and overly optimistic timetables, companies are now flying full-size aircraft, submitting hardware to regulators for certification, building factories, and testing routes with prospective customers.

Among the top three U.S. developers of electric planes, Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation are concentrating on piloted vertical-takeoff-and-landing air taxis, otherwise known as eVTOLs. Beta Technologies is taking a broader—and in some ways more innovative—path into the market. Rather than betting first on air taxis, Beta is looking to enter electric aviation through short-haul freight planes that use conventional runways, fed by an open charging network that’s designed to make electric aircraft—both Beta’s and its competitors’—part of a working transportation system.

According to recent reports, to that end, the firm is developing two variants of its Alia airframe: the runway-based CX300 I’m flying in and the A250, which adds four lift propellers for vertical takeoff and landing. Beta claims its test pilots have flown the Alia family more than 300,000 kilometers, including doing multiple U.S. crossings and overseas demonstrations. The company claims an order and option-to-buy backlog of 991 aircraft.

RELATED: From Hockey Enforcer to High-Flying eVTOL CEO.

It has been revealed that “We’re taking a pragmatic stepwise approach for both certification and market entry,” notes Beta’s CEO and founder Kyle Clark. “We’re ready to go today with medical and cargo aircraft that fly from airport to airport.” Next up, he says, will be passenger aircraft with conventional takeoff and landing, followed by cargo eVTOLs, and finally passenger eVTOLs.

Sources indicate that beta’s 17,500-square-meter production facility sits beside the Burlington airport and looks more like a giant sunlit workshop than a conventional airplane factory. Geothermal heat pumps help heat and cool the structure. The roof will eventually hold a megawatt of solar panels. On the floor, technicians make composite structures and join aircraft sections beneath American and Pride flags.

According to recent reports, 3 Competing Paths to Electric AviationThe top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.aspect_ratioJoby Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger S4 aircraft has six tilting propellers to provide both vertical lift and cruise propulsion. It’s optimized for fast, quiet air-taxi service. The company is also working on hydrogen fuel cells for longer-range transport. Joby claims the S4 is in the final stage of the Federal Aviation Administration’s certification process and has flown trials in Dubai, Latest York, and Texas.Archer Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger Midnight has 12 propellers—six tilting rotors and six stationary rotors. The aircraft, which Archer has been testing in both vertical and conventional takeoffs and landings, is aimed at air-taxi service in urban areas. The company says Midnight is in Phase 4 of the FAA certification process and has completed trial flights.Beta Technologies’ piloted Alia aircraft comes in two flavors: The A250 eVTOL has separate vertical-lift rotors and a rear cruise propeller, while the CX300 is a conventional-takeoff fixed-wing plane. The two models use the same pusher motor, battery pack, flight control computer, and fixed-pitch propeller. The company is initially focusing on cargo and medical transport, regional logistics, and airport-to-airport operations, with passenger service later. Beta expects FAA certification for the CX300 in 2027 and for the A250 a year later.Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.The other major reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”How Redundancy Enhances SafetyA decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.The two versions of Beta’s Alia aircraft—the A250 [shown] and the CX300—share many of the same components, which the company believes will speed up FAA certification.Beta TechnologiesBecause individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.Innovation in eVTOLsBeta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation. Beta Technologies, Made in Vermont Beta TechnologiesAccording to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a big part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company right now employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

According to recent reports, beta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.

According to recent reports, “One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” claims Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.

Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.

There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation.

Sources indicate that according to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a massive part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The manufacturer at the moment employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.

Sources indicate that as befits an aviation manufacturer, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

Electric-aircraft makers compensate with redundant motors and electrical channels, but most leading designs also have wings to allow gliding. In Beta’s A250, that means that if all else fails, the pilot still has a shot at reaching a suitable landing spot.

It has been revealed that that helps explain the convergence in today’s eVTOL designs. Joby Aviation’s S4 uses six propellers that tilt between lift and cruise. Archer Aviation’s Midnight has six tilting propellers and six dedicated lift props. Beta’s A250 keeps its four lift propellers horizontal and uses a separate pusher motor for forward flight.

Sources indicate that in Beta’s home state of Vermont, the electricity produced in the state comes almost entirely from renewable sources. Of course, electric aviation’s climate advantage depends not only on how clean the power grid is, but on how efficiently the aircraft uses energy. The turbines in conventional jet engines are marvelous machines, but they throw away a lot of energy as heat. Plus they need to carry the hardware to manage that heat—inlets, ducts, radiators, oil coolers—and the drag that comes with pulling air through all of it.

Sources indicate that kyle Clark [in cockpit], founder and CEO of Beta Technologies, pilots the firm’s Alia CX300, an electric plane that Beta expects to receive FAA certification in 2027. Clark began designing a hybrid electric plane while still in college.Beta Technologies.

By contrast, an electric design, with no combustion, gearbox, or oil circuits, avoids much of that energy burden. The result is an aircraft that is more than twice as “slippery” in terms of its lift-to-drag ratio. Batteries will never come close to the fuel density of petroleum fuels. But because electric drivetrains are much more efficient than combustion engines, a battery doesn’t necessarily need to match the energy density of petroleum fuel to be useful.

While the motors on an electric aircraft provide the drama at takeoff and landing, the batteries set nearly every boundary: the range, payload, charge time, cooling load, reserve energy, and, ultimately, useful life. For now, the hardest limit on electric aviation is not imagination, software, or even motors. It is the stubborn weight of stored energy.

According to recent reports, “One thing you notice about [electric] airplanes is that they are all small,” says Cecutta, the aviation analyst. “They are not small because someone has done a market study and decided that is the optimal size. They are small because you cannot make them major. This limitation is from the batteries.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a conventional aircraft, fuel accounts for a significant percentage of the takeoff weight. But that weight gradually disappears during flight. In an electric plane, the battery packs also account for a lot of the weight; in Beta’s CX300, they’re close to half the aircraft’s mass. But a drained battery at landing weighs the same as a fully charged one at takeoff. That means the rest of the aircraft must be light enough to lift a power source that never gets lighter, yet strong enough to endure vibration, turbulence, hard landings, and years of fatigue. The more engineers push to save weight, Datta notes, the more flexible the airframe becomes, making the wings and other structures more prone to bending, twisting, and vibration. In that sense, the battery problem becomes a structural problem, too.

Beta’s CX300 carries five liquid-cooled battery packs of about 45 kilowatt-hours each, giving the aircraft roughly 225 kWh of rated capacity, though not all of that may be usable in flight. Each pack weighs 255 kg and contains 2,772 cylindrical cells. Altogether, about 14,000 cells sit beneath the occupied cabin, each one a tiny storehouse of energy, heat, and potential trouble.

The burden of the battery explains much of what I see elsewhere in Beta’s aircraft: the 15-meter wingspan, the composite structure, and the almost doctrinal effort to leave out every piece of hardware and creature comfort that’s not essential to the mission. The CX300 even does without flaps, which most aircraft use to generate extra lift at low speeds, so it must take off and land unusually fast for an aircraft of its size.

On Beta’s battery line, commercially supplied standard 21-millimeter-diameter, 70-mm-long cells are tested and assembled. Cells become modules, modules become subpacks, and eleven subpacks become a 45-kWh pack. Cooling plates manage heat during normal operation, while passive barriers and electrical isolation are designed to contain the ugly edge cases that Beta’s testing process intentionally triggers.

The modular design of the packs will give Beta’s planes a path to better batteries as the cells and battery chemistry improve. Caputo tells me that the manufacturer is already evaluating higher-density cells at its battery testing facility in nearby St. Albans, Vt. More watt-hours per kilogram could eventually mean more range, more payload, or both.

What sets Beta Technologies apart from its competitors is the breadth of its ambitions: It’s not just building electric aircraft. It’s also cultivating a broader ecosystem to nurture the growth of electric aviation.

For instance, Beta intends its motor business to extend beyond its own aircraft. The firm has delivered lift motors for Eve Air Mobility’s proof-of-concept aircraft and has a contract to supply up to $1 billion in pusher motors as Eve’s program develops. In addition, Beta is selling flight-control computers and software to Horizon Aircraft. It is also producing propulsion systems for the military, as well as the MV250, a hybrid-electric autonomous aircraft for defense missions.

Beta’s fast-charging stations [left] have been installed at 138 locations. The thermal-management station [right] keeps the battery from overheating during charging. The company uses the open-standard Combined Charging System (CCS) so that other aircraft can use its chargers. Beta Technologies.

Industry observers note that further evidence of Beta’s far-ranging plans is visible near the battery line in the South Burlington facility, where workers are readying a few of the organization’s 1.5-meter-tall Charge Cubes for shipping. Intended for installation at airports, each cube takes 480-volt AC from the grid and can deliver up to 320 kW at as much as 1,000 volts DC. According to Beta, charging either model of its Alia aircraft takes about 35 minutes, from the minimum charge required under visual flight rules to full state. A separate thermal-management cube circulates water-glycol coolant through the aircraft to keep the batteries from overheating during charging.

The charge cubes use the Combined Charging System (CCS), an open standard increasingly shared across the electric transportation industry. Beta’s strategy resembles Tesla’s decision to treat charging as part of the vehicle business, with one important difference: Beta is courting other aircraft makers, airports, and operators to use its technology. Archer, Atlantic Aviation, Signature Aviation, and government agencies have purchased or installed Beta’s charging equipment. As of October, Beta has 138 fast-charge locations, with additional sites in permitting or construction.

For charging beyond the fixed network, Beta offers a wheeled 40-kW Mini Cube and a 65-kW Mini Cube+ that can ride inside an Alia and plug into more modest electrical service. The Mini Cube can also charge cars, buses, and trucks—any vehicle that uses the CCS standard.

Recent findings suggest that back above Lake Champlain, the CX300 levels off, and the motor recedes to a faint hum. Then Caputo switches it off, and there’s nothing but the rush of wind around the canopy. The aircraft glides on its long wings while the coasting propeller turns the motor into a generator, feeding about 9 kW back to the battery.

Recent findings suggest that then we turn to the east and slip into the landing queue behind a National Guard C-130 Hercules, and Caputo powers and slides the throttle forward. The motor springs to life again, pushing the airplane, and perhaps aviation itself, into the future.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that conor Sheeran is a Movies and TV features writer for Collider. He has a deep passion for cinema and watches everything from the biggest blockbusters to the smallest indies. While he specializes in movies and television, he has also written about politics, culture, and sports throughout his career. Based in Fresh York City, Conor is also a massive fan of the New York Jets, Mets, and Knicks. He is still waiting for any of those teams to bring home a championship in his lifetime. A member of the National Writers Union and the International Federation of Journalists, Conor is a strong proponent of press freedom and collective action.

Heist films are one of cinema's most timeless genres. Whether set in modern times, the 1960s, or the deep past, a good movie about people willing to break the law in exciting ways remains one of the most reliable forms of filmmaking. As Michael B. Jordan prepares to introduce audiences to a latest and updated version of a Hollywood classic, the original film that served as its inspiration is now available to stream for free.

Recent findings suggest that premiering in 1968, The Thomas Crown Affair stars Steve McQueen and Faye Dunaway in one of the best heist movies ever made, and one that remains endlessly cool decades after release. The movie inspired another remake in 1999, starring Pierce Brosnan and Rene Russo, which swapped the original's bank robbery for a more elaborate art theft, something that Jordan's upcoming remake seems to be incorporating. With Jordan's upcoming adaptation starring himself alongside Adria Arjona set to release early in 2027, there's no better time to revisit the original classic. Fortunately for audiences, it is now available to stream for free on platforms including Tubi, Pluto TV, and Roku.

Recent findings suggest that the central plot of The Thomas Crown Affair centers on Thomas Crown (McQueen), a wealthy businessman who appears to have everything anyone could want: He's handsome, successful, and enjoys a luxury lifestyle that many can only dream of. Despite his success, Crown finds himself incredibly bored with his comfortable existence. This boredom manifests itself in a rather interesting way: he orchestrates an elaborate bank robbery, despite having no need for the money. Unlike traditional crime thrillers that tend to follow criminals who are down on their luck or desperate for money, The Thomas Crown Affair introduces a criminal who is motivated entirely by the thrill of getting away with something extraordinary.

According to recent reports, crown's confidence is soon challenged by an investigator, Vicki Anderson (Dunaway), who begins looking into the robbery to discover who could be behind the audacious crime. What follows is a cat-and-mouse game between Crown and Anderson, leading both to realize the romantic attraction that builds as each learns more about the other. It's a fascinating psychological battle between two intelligent adversaries, a duel that is only more exciting to watch thanks to the performances of McQueen and Dunaway. McQueen's effortlessly charismatic performance exudes cool, and it's easy to see how someone could be swayed by his charm, while Dunaway is the perfect foil. She knows what it would take to stop a man like Crown, but she also struggles to resist the temptation to be with him.

It has been revealed that the enduring appeal of a story like The Thomas Crown Affair extends far beyond just McQueen and Dunaway's performances. Norman Jewison's direction gives the film a sleek, immersive style through its split-screen photography and editing, creating a distinctive look. The styling, costumes, on-set location shoots, and incredible score set the stage for an unforgettable experience. The Thomas Crown Affair helped establish a format for films like Ocean's Eleven and Entrapment that followed later, so it's easy to see how timeless this movie is and why a modern remake makes sense.

It has been revealed that michael B. Jordan's remake will take inspiration from the original and the 1999 version with Pierce Brosnan and Rene Russo, swapping a bank robbery for art thefts. This will mark Jordan's second time in the director's chair following Creed III; he will also produce and star alongside Adria Arjona, Kenneth Branagh, and Lily Gladstone. While many heist movies emphasize action, often using it as the anchor for the project, The Thomas Crown Affair demonstrates that compelling characters with psychological tension can be just as entertaining. The greatest strength of both films was the romantic and sexual tension between their leads, and, judging by the trailers, Jordan seems to be following in their footsteps.

It has been revealed that jordan's interpretation will certainly bring its own unique perspective to the source material, but the original film with McQueen and Dunaway remains a must-watch and the gold standard. For those eager to sink their teeth into a good heist movie and see the one that started it all, it's available to stream and, best of all, it's free on Tubi, Pluto TV, and Roku. Needless to say, McQueen's crime thriller is still essential viewing even nearly 60 years later.

Siri Modular, the upcoming Apple Watch face in watchOS 27, is gaining new style options. watchOS 27.3, at the moment in beta, adds two more style options to the existing set. This gives customers five options for adjusting what type of information appears on Siri Modular.

Sources indicate that siri Modular originally shipped with three style options. Each supports a small line complication above the time.

Additionally, the original three styles include these options:.

In watchOS 27.3, Apple introduces two latest Siri features that work with Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.

First, there’s Siri Recap which uses the Apple Watch to turn audio into high-level text summaries. Second, there’s Live Rewind which lets you view a transcript of the last 15 seconds of spoken word.

The two newly introduced Siri Modular Apple Watch face styles help surface three things: invoking Siri, viewing conversations with Siri, and viewing Siri Recaps on the Apple Watch.

The latest styles include a pill-shaped module that includes icon shortcuts that go directly to Siri conversations, invoke Siri AI, or go directly to Siri Recaps in the Siri app.

One style features a large digital clock with the fresh three-button Siri module. Another includes a compact digital clock with a Smart Stack tile and the new three-button Siri module.

This brings the style options to five. If you use the three circular complications configuration, you can also assign a Siri icon that invokes Siri AI.

watchOS 27.3 is at the moment in beta and expected to be released officially in December.
